translation:
Page 157

[Left column:]
...arising from nail-wounds, and swellings caused by poison, wind, and heat arising from contact — these arise. They are recognized by their own characteristic signs and symptoms. Those caused by external factors, when treated partially with wound-bandaging, mantras, medicinal pastes and plasters, fomentations, and other such measures, subside. But those of internal origin are properly resolved through the appropriate application of oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, enema, and nasal therapies; or they may worsen through improper dietary combinations. Conditions such as vomiting, fainting, cough, asthma, diarrhea, wasting, pallor, fever, abdominal disorders, prolapse, fistula, and hemorrhoids arise from improper suppression. Also from conditions such as skin diseases, itching, and eruptions; or from suppression of the urges of semen, flatus, urine, and feces; or in one who is emaciated from fasting and skin disease — through sudden consumption of heavy, very salty, ground preparations, fruits, vegetables, radish, green herbs, honey, alcohol, coarse grains, aquatic and marshy foods, meat; from eating clay or unripe things in excess; from compression of the fetus, premature delivery, and from improper treatment of newborns — swellings arise. These are the general causes.

[Right column:]
Now, the specific causes are as follows: Wind (Vata), aggravated by cold, rough, light, poison, fasting, excessive exercise, throwing, and similar factors, overpowers the skin, flesh, blood, and other tissues and produces swelling. It subsides when the patient lies down. Its color is dusky or reddish; it is unsteady in nature, pulsating, rough, and coarse; the skin and hair become loose; there is a feeling of being pierced, pricked with needles, as if ants are crawling over it; it feels like sesame seeds are being scattered; there is tingling; it contracts and stretches — this is Vata-type swelling.

Pitta, aggravated by hot, sharp, pungent, alkaline, salty, stale food, fire, sun, and heat exposure, overpowers the skin, flesh, blood, and other tissues and produces swelling. It subsides when the patient lies down. It is blackish, yellowish, blue, or copper-colored in appearance; hot, soft, with copper-colored hair; there is burning, throbbing, a sensation of being smoked or steamed, sweating, and intolerance of hot touch — this is Pitta-type swelling.

Kapha, aggravated by heavy, sweet, cold, unctuous foods, excessive sleep, lack of exercise, and similar factors, overpowers the skin, flesh, blood, and other tissues and produces swelling. It is slow in onset and slow to subside...

From the Charaka Samhita.

It becomes so. The pallid-white appearance, unctuous, smooth, heavy, stable, sluggish, white-haired, cold-tolerant, whitish — this is the phlegm-type swelling. According to the combination of their respective causes and forms, swellings arising from two doshas are named after those doshas. Similarly, from the combination of causes of all three, there arises a single tri-doshic type. Thus there are these varieties. And further, there is just one swelling in terms of its general characteristic of elevation. (1)

Now, there are three types of swelling (shopha): those arising from wind (vata), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha). They are further of two kinds — intrinsic (nija) and extrinsic (agantuka). Among these, the extrinsic ones arise from cutting, splitting, scratching, breaking, scraping, pressing, striking, binding, wrapping, crushing, squeezing; or from the flowers, fruits, and juices of plants such as Bhilaya, Atmagupta, Ashruka, worms, Shruka, Ahita, leaf-creepers, tumors, and such contacts; or from the stings, teeth, horns, and claws of venomous and non-venomous creatures; or from contact with sea-poisons, wind, cold, and fire — these give rise to swellings. They are such that, when the signs produced by their own causes first appear, treatments opposite to those signs — such as binding, mantras,

application of medicinal pastes, exposure to breeze, cooling, and similar therapeutic measures — bring about relief. And those that are intrinsic — they manifest from improper use of oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, retention enemas, unctuous enemas, and head-purgation; or from improper combination of treatments; or from vomiting, laziness, cholera, asthma, cough, diarrhea, wasting, anemia, fever, abdominal disorders, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, extreme thirst, skin diseases such as kushtha, itching, eruptions; or from suppression of the urges of vomiting, sneezing (saliva), belching, semen, flatus, urine, and feces; or from skin diseases and fasting; or from consuming food and substances that are very heavy, sour, salty, made of ground grains, fruits, vegetables, sauces, curds, raw vegetables, wines, weak barley preparations, shami-grain, various other grains, and meat from marshy regions; or from excess salt consumption; from compression of the fetus, from miscarriage of an immature fetus, and from improper treatment of born children — from excess of doshas, swelling manifests. Chapter on the Six Substances (Shadrasa-sthana)
(Page 159)

The swelling moves over it like ants (lice), contracts and expands like mustard-paste applied to the skin. This is called Vata-shopha (edematous swelling due to Vata). And when one eats foods that are hot, sharp, pungent, salty, or sour, or when digestion is impaired, or when one is excessively exposed to fire or sunlight, then Pitta becomes aggravated and overpowers the skin, muscle, and blood, producing swelling. This swelling rises and subsides quickly. It is black, yellow, blue, or copper-colored in appearance; it is warm, soft, tawny, copper-colored, and hairless in character. Sensations as if of burning, smoke, heat, perspiration, and pricking seem to arise within it, yet its touch is not hot. This is Pitta-type swelling. And when one is excessively sedentary, fond of sweets, cold things, excessive sleep, and avoids exercise, Kapha becomes aggravated and overpowers the skin, muscle, blood, etc., producing swelling. This swelling rises with difficulty and subsides slowly. It is pale-white in complexion, smooth, heavy, firm, and large. The hair-tips over it appear whitish; it can tolerate hot touch. This is Kapha-type swelling. Just as, through their own causes and combination of features, three types of swelling arise from two doshas together, so also from the simultaneous aggravation of all three doshas (sannipata), one sannipata-type swelling arises. In this way there are seven types in all. Through various combinations of these basic natures, two, three, four, or seven varieties of swelling are found. Yet in their general elevation (puffiness), all are essentially one. || 1 ||

And the following verses apply here:

When a person's limbs seem to throb, feel as if asleep, are painful, and when pressed rise back up again — that swelling is to be called Vata-shopha. || 2 ||

And that swelling which is reddish in color, disappears at night, and is relieved by oleation and hot massage — that too is of the Vata type. || 3 ||

That swelling which occurs in one afflicted by thirst and fever, which burns intensely, causes perspiration, pricking, and has a foul odor — that swelling is known as Pitta-type. || 4 ||

That swelling which first appears in the eyes, face, and skin with a yellow tinge, in which there is a flow in the middle stage, and the skin becomes thin — that is called Pitta-shopha. || 5 ||

Digitized By Slddhanta eGangotri Gyaan Kosha

सूक्ष्म हो और अतिसारको करै–वहभी पित शोफ कहाहै ॥ ५ ॥

य:शीतल:सक्तगति:कण्डुमानपाण्डुरेवच । निपीडितोनोञ्चमितश्वयथु:स कफात्मक: ॥ ६ ॥

जिसकी गतिमें शीत हो खुजली हो पीला हो और दबानेसे ऊपरको उठजाय वह शोथ कफात्मक होताहै ॥ ६ ॥

यस्यशस्त्रकुशचछेदाच्छोणितंनप्रवर्तते । कच्छ्रेणिपच्छानु:स्रव तिसचापिकफसम्भव: ॥ ७ ॥

और शस्त्र कुशासे छेदन किये जिसमेंसे रुधिर न निकसै और कष्टसे पिच्छ जिसमेंसे निकसें वहभी कफसे उत्पन्नहै७

निदानाकृतिसंसर्गात्श्वयथु:स्याद्विदोषज: । सर्वाकृति:सान्निपाताच्छोथोऽग्यामिश्रहेतुज: ॥ ८ ॥

निदान और आकृतिके संसर्गसे दो दोषोंसे उत्पन्न शोथ होताहै सब आकार हों मिलेहुये हेतु हों वह शोफ सांनिपातसे होताहै ॥ ८ ॥

यस्तुपादाभिनिर्वृत्त:शोथ:सर्वाङ्गोभवेत् ।जन्तो:सचसुकष्ट:स्यात्स्रुत:स्त्रीमुखाच्यय: ॥ ९ ॥

जो शोफ पादोंसे चलकर सर्वाँग गामी हो जाय वह शोफ जंतुको आतिकष्ट देताहै और स्त्रीके मुखसे लेकर फैला हो ॥ ९ ॥

यश्चापिगुह्यप्रभव:स्त्रियोवापुरुषस्य वा । सचकष्टमोञ्ञेयोयस्यचस्युरुपद्रवा: ॥ १० ॥

और जो लिंग वा योनिमें स्त्री वा पुरुषके हो और जिसमें उपद्रवहों वह अत्यंत कष्ट दाता जानना ॥ १० ॥

छर्दि:श्वासोऽरुचिस्तृष्णाज्वरोऽतीसारएवच । सप्तकोऽयंसदौर्बल्य:शोथोपद्रवसंग्रह: ॥ ११ ॥

छर्दि श्वास अरुचि तृष्णा, ज्वर अतीसार दुर्बलता ये सात शोकके उपद्रव होतेहैं ॥ ११ ॥

यस्यश्लेष्माणकुपित:जिह्वामूलेऽवतिष्ठते । आशुसञ्जनयञ्छोथंकरोतिगलशुण्डकाम् ॥ १२ ॥

जिसका कुपित हुआ कफ काक पर टिक जाताहै वह शीघ्र शोफको पैदाकरता हुआ, गल शुण्डिकाको पैदा करताहै१२।

यस्यश्लेष्माणकुपितस्तिष्ठत्यन्तर्गलेस्थित: । आशुसञ्जनयञ्छोथंगलगण्डोऽस्यजायते ॥ १३ ॥

और जिसका कुपित कफ गलके भीतर टिकजाय वह शीघ्र शोफको पैदाकरके गल गंड कर देताहै ॥ १३ ॥

यस्यश्लेष्माणकुपितोगलवाहेऽवतिष्ठते । शनै:सञ्जनयञ्छोथंजायतेऽस्यगलग्रह: ॥ १४ ॥

[Verse 5 continued:] ...when it is subtle and also causes diarrhea — that too is called Pittaja Shopha (swelling due to bile). ॥ 5 ॥

Verse 6: That swelling in which the movement is cold, accompanied by itching, pallor, and which rises upward when pressed — that swelling is of the nature of Kapha (phlegm). ॥ 6 ॥

[Commentary on verse 6:] That swelling whose movement is cold, which produces itching, which appears pale, and which rises up when pressed — that swelling is Kaphaja (caused by phlegm). ॥ 6 ॥

Verse 7: That swelling from which, when cut by a sharp instrument or blade of kusha grass, blood does not flow, and from which mucus oozes out only with great difficulty — that too is produced by Kapha. ॥ 7 ॥

[Commentary on verse 7:] When cut by a weapon or kusha grass, blood does not emerge, and only with great difficulty does mucus ooze out — that too is produced by phlegm. ॥ 7 ॥

Verse 8: A swelling arising from the combination of causes and characteristics of two doshas is called Dvandvaja (dual-origin). A swelling that has all characteristics combined, arising from mixed causes, is Sannipataja (arising from all three doshas together). ॥ 8 ॥

[Commentary on verse 8:] A swelling arising from the combination of the causes and characteristics of two doshas is called Dvandvaja. When all characteristics and causes are mixed together, that swelling is of Sannipataja origin. ॥ 8 ॥

Verse 9: That swelling which begins in the feet and becomes generalized throughout the body is very difficult for the patient — and one that spreads starting from a woman's face is similarly grave. ॥ 9 ॥

[Commentary on verse 9:] A swelling that begins in the feet and spreads throughout the entire body gives extreme distress to the patient, and one that spreads beginning from a woman's face is similarly dangerous. ॥ 9 ॥

Verse 10: And swelling that arises in the genitals — whether of a woman or a man — and in which complications appear, should be known as extremely distressing. ॥ 10 ॥

[Commentary on verse 10:] Swelling in the penis or vagina, whether in a woman or a man, and in which there are complications, should be understood as causing extreme distress. ॥ 10 ॥

Verse 11: Vomiting, breathlessness, loss of appetite, thirst, fever, diarrhea, and weakness — these seven are the complications of swelling (shopha). ॥ 11 ॥

[Commentary on verse 11:] Vomiting, breathlessness, loss of appetite, thirst, fever, diarrhea, and weakness — these seven are the complications of swelling. ॥ 11 ॥

Verse 12: When the aggravated Kapha settles at the root of the tongue, it quickly produces swelling and gives rise to tonsillitis (gala-shundika). ॥ 12 ॥

[Commentary on verse 12:] When the aggravated Kapha settles on the uvula, it quickly produces swelling and gives rise to tonsillitis. ॥ 12 ॥

Verse 13: When the aggravated Kapha settles inside the throat, it quickly produces swelling and gives rise to goiter of the throat (gala-ganda). ॥ 13 ॥

[Commentary on verse 13:] When the aggravated Kapha settles inside the throat, it quickly produces swelling and causes a glandular swelling of the throat. ॥ 13 ॥

Verse 14: When the aggravated Kapha settles in the channel of the throat, it slowly produces swelling and gives rise to constriction of the throat (gala-graha). ॥ 14 ॥

translation:
Page 161 — Sutrasthana (Chapter on General Principles)

[Verse 14]
When aggravated phlegm (kapha) remains lodged outside the throat, it gradually produces swelling and causes obstruction of the throat (galagrah).

[Verse 15 — Sanskrit]
When pitta becomes aggravated together with blood and spreads through the skin, it gives rise to swelling with redness (raga) and spreading inflammation (visarpa).

[Verse 15 — Commentary]
When one's aggravated pitta, along with blood, spreads through the skin, it produces redness and swelling and causes erysipelas (visarpa).

[Verse 16 — Sanskrit]
When aggravated pitta settles in the skin along with blood, it produces redness and swelling and gives rise to pustular eruptions (pindaka).

[Verse 16 — Commentary]
When one's aggravated pitta, together with blood, settles in the skin, it produces swelling and redness and gives rise to pustular eruptions.

[Verse 17 — Sanskrit]
When aggravated pitta settles in the temporal regions (shankhau), a terrible swelling called Shankhaka arises there.

[Verse 17 — Commentary]
When one's aggravated pitta settles in the temples, a terrible swelling named Shankhaka arises there.

[Verse 18 — Sanskrit]
When aggravated pitta settles at the root of the ear, a fatal and incurable swelling arises at the end of fever.

[Verse 18 — Commentary]
When one's aggravated pitta settles at the root of the ear, the swelling that arises at the end of fever becomes an incurable, life-threatening condition.

[Verse 19 — Sanskrit]
When aggravated vata becomes lodged by pushing the spleen (steeha) upward, the spleen grows larger while causing piercing pain in the sides.

[Verse 19 — Commentary]
When the spleen is pushed upward and aggravated vata becomes lodged there, the spleen enlarges while inflicting pain in the flanks.

[Verse 20 — Sanskrit]
When aggravated vata becomes lodged in the region of a gulma (abdominal lump), it produces swelling with pain, and a gulma tumor arises.

[Verse 20 — Commentary]
When one's aggravated vata settles in the gulma regions, it produces swelling with pain and gives rise to gulma disease.

[Verse 21 — Sanskrit]
When aggravated vata, producing swelling and pain, travels from the groin (vankshana) to the scrotum (vrushana), it becomes bound there and a scrotal swelling (vrishma/vriddhi) arises.

[Verse 21 — Commentary]
When one's aggravated vata, causing swelling and pain, travels from the groin to the testes, a scrotal swelling results.

[Verse 22 — Sanskrit]
When aggravated vata takes shelter between the skin and the muscles, producing swelling in the abdominal cavity (kukshi), abdominal disease (udara) arises.

[Verse 22 — Commentary]
When one's aggravated vata settles between the skin and muscle and produces swelling, it gives rise to abdominal disease in the abdominal cavity.

( १६२ )

यस्यवातःप्रकुपितःकुक्षिमाश्रित्य
तिष्ठति । नाधोव्रजतिनाप्यूर्ध्वंञा
नाहस्तस्यजायते ॥ २३ ॥

जिसका कुपित वात कुक्षिके आश्रय
से टिकै न नीचे जाय न ऊपर जाय
उसके आनाह ( अफरा ) होजाताहै२३

रोगाश्चोत्सेधसामान्यादिधमांसा
र्बुदादयः। विशिष्टानामरूपाभ्यां
निर्देश्याःशोथसंग्रहे ॥ २४ ॥

और उंचाईके सामान्यसे अधिमांस
अर्बुद आदि रोग वे होतेहैं जो विशिष्ट
नाम रूपसे शोक संग्रहमें कहेहैं ॥२४॥

वातपित्तकफायस्थयुगपत्कुपिता
ञ्रयः । जिह्वामूलेऽवतिष्ठन्तेविद
हन्तःसमुच्छ्रताः ॥ २५ ॥

जिसके वात पित्त कफ तीनों एकबार
कुपित हों और जिह्वाके मूलमें टिकै
विदाह करते हुए बद्जांय वे अत्यंत
शोफको पैदा करतेहैं ॥ २५ ॥

जनयन्तिभृशंशोथंवेदनाश्चपृथ
ग्विधाः। तंशीघ्रकारिणंरोगंरोहि
णीकेतिनिर्दिशेत् ॥ २६ ॥

और अतिशोथ और अनेक प्रकारकी
वेदना करतेहैं उस शीघ्र कारी रोगको
रोहिणीका कहतेहैं ॥ २६ ॥

त्रिरात्रंपरमंतस्यजन्तोर्भवतिजी
वितम् । कुशलेनत्वनुषाताःक्षिप्रं
सम्पद्यतेसुखी ॥ २७ ॥

उस जंतुका परेसे परे तीन रात्रि
जीवन होताहै और कुशल वैद्य माप्त
होजाय तो शीघ्र सुखी होजाताहै॥२७॥

सन्तिह्येवंविधारोगाःसाध्यादारु
णसम्मताः । येह्न्युरनुपकान्ता
मिथ्यारम्भेणवापुनः ॥ २८ ॥

इस प्रकारके दारुण संमत(माने)साध्य
रोगहैं जो चिकित्साके न करनेसे वा
मिथ्या चिकित्सा करनेसे मार देतेहैं२८

साध्याश्चाप्यपरेहन्तिव्याधयोमृ
दुसम्मताः । यत्नायत्नकृतंयेषुक
मैसिध्यत्यसंशयम् ॥ २९ ॥

और अपर मृदु संमत साध्य व्याधि
भी हैं जिनमें यत्न अयत्नसे किया कर्म
निःसंदेह सिद्ध होताहै ॥ २९ ॥

असाध्याश्चापरेसन्तिव्याधयोया
प्यसंज्ञिताः । सुसाध्येऽपिकृतंये
षुकर्मयाप्यकरंभवेत् ॥ ३० ॥

और जिस मनुष्यके असाध्य नामकी
अपरव्याधि व्याप्यहै सुसाध्य होनेपरभी
जिनमें किया हुआ कर्म याप्य सिद्धिका
कारक होताहै ॥ ३० ॥

सन्तिचाप्यपरेरोगाःकर्मयेषुनिस
ध्यति। अपियत्नकृतंवचैनतान्वि
द्वानुपाचरेत् ॥ ३१ ॥

और अपर रोग ऐसेभीहैं जिनमें कर्म
सिद्ध नहीं होता चाहे वह यत्नसेभी
किया जाय विद्वान् मनुष्य उनकी
चिकित्सा न करै ॥ ३१ ॥
translation:
(162)

[Verse 23]
When the aggravated vata takes up residence in the abdomen and moves neither downward nor upward, the condition known as anaha (abdominal distension/flatulence) arises in that person.

[Commentary 23]
When the aggravated vata becomes lodged in the abdomen, moving neither downward nor upward, the condition called anaha (bloating/flatulence) occurs in that person.

[Verse 24]
Diseases such as excessive swellings, flesh-tumors (arbuda), and the like — which arise from common causes such as raised swellings — are to be described by their specific names and characteristics in the chapter on swellings (shotha-sangraha).

[Commentary 24]
Diseases such as excessive swelling and arbuda (tumors) are those that are described by their specific names and characteristics in the chapter on swellings.

[Verse 25]
When vata, pitta, and kapha are all simultaneously aggravated and become lodged at the root of the tongue, causing a burning sensation and rising upward, they produce extreme swelling.

[Commentary 25]
When all three — vata, pitta, and kapha — are simultaneously aggravated and lodge at the root of the tongue, producing burning and becoming obstructed, they create extreme swelling.

[Verse 26]
They produce severe swelling and diverse types of pain. This rapidly acting disease is known as rohini.

[Commentary 26]
They produce extreme swelling and many types of pain. This rapidly advancing disease is called rohini.

[Verse 27]
The maximum survival of such a patient is three nights. But if a skilled physician is obtained promptly, the person soon recovers and becomes well.

[Commentary 27]
The maximum lifespan of such a patient is three nights. But if a skilled physician is found quickly, the patient soon becomes well.

[Verse 28]
There are diseases of this terrible kind that are reckoned as curable (sadhya), yet they can be fatal when left untreated or treated incorrectly.

[Commentary 28]
Such dreadful diseases that are considered curable can kill when not treated or when treated wrongly.

[Verse 29]
There are other diseases classified as mildly curable (mridu-sadhya), in which treatment applied either with great effort or with little effort undoubtedly succeeds.

[Commentary 29]
There are other diseases called mildly curable in which treatment — whether undertaken with great care or casually — succeeds without doubt.

[Verse 30]
There are still other diseases called asadhya (incurable) and yapya (palliable). Even in diseases that are easily curable, when these are also present, any treatment performed merely becomes palliative.

[Commentary 30]
When a person has a disease that is called incurable alongside one that is easily curable, even the treatment of the curable one yields only palliative results.

[Verse 31]
And there are still other diseases in which treatment yields no results at all. Even if effort is made, a learned physician should not undertake their treatment.

[Commentary 31]
There are other diseases in which no cure is achieved, even with great effort. A learned person should not attempt to treat such diseases.

translation:
(Page 163)

Verse 32:
Diseases are of two kinds: curable (sadhya) and incurable (asadhya). By the distinction of mild (mridu) and severe (daruna), they become four kinds in all.
Commentary: Diseases have been described as two types — curable and incurable. By the further division into mild and severe, they become four types altogether. (32)

Verse 33:
These same diseases, when further enumerated, become countless, being distinguished by their causative factors (nidana), symptoms (vedana), color (varna), site (sthana), configuration (samsthana), and name (nama).
Commentary: Those same diseases, when further subdivided, become innumerable — they are differentiated by cause, symptom, color, site, form, and name. (33)

Verse 34:
The principle governing their classification, as summarized among gross diseases, is similarly applied to natural constitutional disorders.
Commentary: The reason for their classification is this: just as there is a general grouping among gross diseases, similarly it is described for constitutional disorders. (34)

Verse 35:
A physician who is unskilled in the names of diseases should never be ashamed, for there is no fixed and certain knowledge to be derived from the names of all diseases alone.
Commentary: A physician who is not conversant with the names of diseases should never feel embarrassed, because mere knowledge of all disease names does not by itself lead to definitive understanding. (35)

Verse 36:
The same aggravated dosha, by virtue of the specific nature of its origin and by moving to other sites, gives rise to many diseases.
Commentary: That same aggravated dosha, by reason of the specific nature of its provocation and by migrating to other locations, produces many diseases. (36)

Verse 37:
Therefore, knowing the nature of the disorders, the subsidiary seats, and the specific modes of origin, the physician should undertake treatment accordingly.
Commentary: Thus, knowing the nature of the disorders, the other seats, and the particularities of their origins, the physician should administer treatment. (37)

Verse 38:
A physician who knows these three things and then undertakes therapeutic action proceeds with knowledge and according to proper method, and is not deluded in his practice.
Commentary: The physician who knows these three and then initiates treatment acts with knowledge and in accordance with proper reasoning, and thus is not confused in his actions. (38)

Verse 39:
Vata, pitta, kapha, and blood are permanently present in the bodies of living beings. Whether they are in a disordered state or in their natural state — a wise person should desire to know them in this way.
Commentary: Vata, pitta, kapha, and blood are always present in the bodies of living beings; whether they are disturbed or in their natural condition, a learned person should wish to understand them as such. (39)

Verse 40:
Enthusiasm, inhalation, exhalation, bodily movement, uniform movement of the tissues, and equal discharge — these are the normal (non-disordered) functions of vata in those who possess movement.
Commentary: Enthusiasm, upward breath, downward breath, physical effort, uniform movement of the dhatus, and equal release — these are the normal, undisturbed functions of vata in moving beings. (40)

translation:
( 162 )

[Verse 41]
Sight, digestion, warmth, bright eyes, softness of the body, lustre, clarity of mind, and intelligence — these are the normal (non-disordered) functions arising from pitta. (41)

Commentary: Sight, digestion, warmth, moisture, softness, lustre, clarity of mind, intelligence — these are the undisturbed normal actions of pitta. (41)

[Verse 42]
Unctuousness, binding, stability, heaviness, virility, strength, forbearance, steadiness of mind, and freedom from greed — these are the normal functions arising from kapha. (42)

Commentary: Unctuousness, binding, stability, heaviness, virility, strength, forbearance, steadiness, absence of greed — these are the undisturbed normal functions of kapha. (42)

[Verse 43]
When vata, pitta, and kapha are diminished, their characteristics are described. Or when the natural functions of the doshas become deficient or antagonistic, that too is described. (43)

Commentary: When vata, pitta, and kapha are in a state of diminution, their characteristics are described; when the natural functions of the doshas are impaired or when antagonisms arise, that is also described. (43)

[Verse 44]
The specific peculiarity of the constitution of the doshas is a definite sign of their increase. The examination of whether the doshas are in their natural state, or diminished, or increased, is thus carried out. (44)

Commentary: The unevenness in the constitution of the doshas is a definite indicator of their increase; the examination of the natural state, diminution, or increase of the doshas is performed accordingly. (44)

[Summary verse 45]
In those verses — the count, the causes, the forms of edemas (shotha), their incurability, and a three-fold summary of knowledge regarding each of those disorders. (45)

translation:
(166)

Diseases arising from the combination of vata, pitta, and kapha together, as well as those arising from each individually. The five dietary prohibitions relate to vata, pitta, and kapha aversions. The five head diseases, as enumerated earlier, include those caused by vata, pitta, kapha, and their combination, as well as those of glandular origin. The five heart diseases are explained in the same manner as the head diseases. The five types of anemia (pandu) arise from vata, pitta, kapha, their combination, and from clay-eating. The five types of mental disorder (unmada) arise from vata, pitta, kapha, their combination, and from extraneous causes. The four eye diseases, four ear diseases, four types of wasting, four mouth diseases, four disorders of the digestive tract (grahani), four types of intoxication (mada), and four types of fainting (murccha) are explained under epilepsy (apasmara). The four types of wasting (shosa) arise from overexertion, suppression of urges, depletion, and irregular eating. The four types of sexual debility arise from injury to the seed, fracture of the organ, and from decay of the vital essence. The three types of edema (shotha) are caused by vata, pitta, and kapha respectively. The three types of skin discoloration (kalasa) are copper-red, white, and tawny. The three forms of blood-pitta disorder are classified by location: upper, lower, and both together.

The two types of fever: one arising from heat exposure with cold as its cause, and one from cold exposure with heat as its cause. The two types of wounds: those of internal origin and those from external causes. The two types of exertion: external and internal. The two types of visual disorder (gridhrasyi): one caused by vata alone, and one by vata combined with kapha. The two types of jaundice (kamala): one seated in the viscera and one in the channels. The two forms of indigestion (ama): sluggish digestion (alasaka) and acute gastroenteritis (visuchika). The two forms of blood-disorder (vatarakta): deep-seated and superficial. The two types of facial paralysis (ardita): moist and dry. The single type of urinary obstruction (urustambha) arises from all three doshas combined. The single condition called sanyasa (complete collapse of consciousness) is tridoshic in nature, manifesting in both mind and body. The one great disease is false conviction (atattva-abhinivesha). The twenty types of parasitic organisms: lice and ants — these two are external, born of bodily impurities; those that feed on hair, on body hair, on skin patches, on serous fluid, and on blood — these six are blood-born; those dwelling in the intestines, abdomen, and heart, including the churvoda, darbha-flower worm, saugandhika, and mahaguda — these seven are kapha-born; the kakeruka, makeruka, leliha, sthulaka, and sausurada — these five are born of feces. Thus there are twenty classes of parasitic organisms. Twenty —

The pramehas (urinary disorders): udaka-meha, shveta-meha, rasa-meha, sandra-meha, sandraprasada-meha, shukla-meha, shukla-meha, shita-meha, shanair-meha, sikata-meha, and lala-meha — these ten are caused by kapha (phlegm).
Kshara-meha, kala-meha, nila-meha, lohita-meha, manjishtha-meha, and haridra-meha — these six are caused by pitta (bile).
Vasa-meha, majja-meha, hasti-meha, and madhu-meha — these four are caused by vata (wind). Thus there are twenty pramehas.
The twenty yoni-vyapads (disorders of the female reproductive tract): vatika, paittika, shlaishmika, and sannipatika — these four are caused by the doshas. Sixteen are described by their characteristics of dushya, samsarga, and prakriti. These are: rakta-yoni, rajaska, acharana, atichrana, prakcharana, upashuta, udavartini, karnini, puchrandni, antarmukhi, suchimukhi, shushka, vamini, shandayoni, and mahayoni — these twenty yoni-vyapads are mentioned here only as a listing; they will be described fully in their respective places.

And there is a verse on this:
Twenty, one, three, and three; two, eight, four, ten, twelve, and five groups; four groups of eight, six, two, and hundreds — these are all illuminated in the chapter on the eight abdominal diseases. (1)

translation:
( 168 )
In the Charaka Samhita

[Arising from] sugar-crystals, semen, and blood — the eight defects of milk are: discoloration, bad smell, tastelessness, sliminess, frothiness, roughness, heaviness, and excessive unctuousness. The eight defects of semen are: thinness, dryness, frothiness, lack of whiteness, sliminess, admixture with other tissues, and sediment. The seven [types of skin conditions] are: kapala, udumbara, mandala, rishya, jihva, pundarika, and sidhma-kakinika. The seven types of pindakas are: sharavika, kachchhipaka, jalini, sarshapi, alaji, vinata, and vidradhi. The seven types of visarpa [spreading skin eruptions] are: arising from vata, pitta, kapha, agni, kardama, granthi, and sannipata. The six [types of] atisara [diarrhea] are: arising from vata, pitta, kapha, sannipata, fear, and edema. Udavarta [upward movement of wind] arises from vata, urine, feces, semen, vomiting, and swelling. The five gulmas [abdominal tumors] arise from vata, pitta, kapha, sannipata, and blood — these are called the five gulma defects. The five types of kasa [cough] arise from vata, pitta, kapha, injury, and wasting — these are: mahan, urdhva, chhinna, tamaka, and kshudra. The five types of shvasa [breathing disorders] are: mahati, gambhira, vyapeta, kshudra, and those arising from food. The five types of trishna [thirst] are: from vata, pitta, ama, wasting, and as a complication. The five types of chhardi [vomiting] arise from consumption of disagreeable food and from aggravation of vata, pitta, kapha, and their combination. The five conditions related to fasting and eating are caused by vata, pitta, kapha, aversion, and exertion. The five types of shiro-roga [head diseases] arise — as stated in the earlier enumeration — from vata, pitta, kapha, sannipata, and parasites. The five hrid-rogas [heart diseases] are to be understood similarly to head diseases.

The five types of pandu-roga [anemia/jaundice] arise from vata, pitta, kapha, sannipata, and eating clay. The five types of unmada [mental disorders] arise from vata, pitta, kapha, sannipata, and external causes. The four types of apasmara [epilepsy] arise from vata, pitta, kapha, and sannipata. There are four eye diseases, four ear diseases, four types of pratishyaya [catarrh], four types of mouth diseases, four types of grahani [intestinal] disorders, four types of mada [intoxication], and four types of murccha [fainting] — all of these are described under the heading of apasmara. The four types of shosha [consumption/wasting] arise from recklessness, suppression of urges, and irregular eating. The four types of klaibya [impotence] are: destruction of semen, collapse of the phallus, old age, and diminution of semen. The three types of shopha [edema] arise from vata, pitta, and kapha. The three types of kilasa [a skin disorder] are distinguished by their location: upper region, lower region, and both regions. There are three types of lohita-pitta [a bleeding disorder]. The two types of jwara [fever] are: one arising from heat and one from cold — though the one arising from a cold tendency may also arise from heat. The two types of vrana [wounds/ulcers] are: those arising internally and those caused by external injury. The two types of ayama [spasm] are: external and internal. The two types of gridhrasi [sciatica] are: from vata alone and from vata combined with kapha. The two types of kamala [jaundice] are: kosthashrita [located in the viscera] and shakashrita [located in the peripheral channels]. The two types of ama [undigested toxic matter] are: alasaka and vimuchika. The two types of vatarakta [gout] are distinguished as deep and superficial. Arsha [hemorrhoids] are of two types based on whether they are moist or dry. Arustambha [a disease of stiffness and cracking] is one condition arising from ama and the three doshas. Sannyasa [coma/collapse] is one condition arising from all three doshas, manifesting in both mind and body — and it is one [such condition].

The great disease [mahagada] is this: that the fundamental elements do not find their proper seat. There are twenty classes of parasitic organisms [krimi]: lice [yuka] and ants [pipilika] — these two arise from the external secretions of the body. [Others such as] Keshad, Lomad, Lomadvipa, Saurasa, Audumbara — these organisms in general, six in number, are born from blood. From the intestines, the abdomen, wandering in the heart, [and other sites arise] Pushpa, Saugandhika, Mahaguda — these seven arise from phlegm [kapha]. Kakeruka, Makeruka, Leliha, Sazhulaka, Sausura — these five arise in feces. These are the twenty classes of parasitic organisms.

The twenty types of urinary disorders [prameha] are as follows: Udakameha, Ikshameha, Rasameha, Sandhrameha, Sandhraprasadameha, Shukrameha, Shitameha, Shanaimeha, Sikatameha, Lalameh — these ten arise due to kapha. Ksharameha, Kalameha, Nilameha, Chohitameha, Manjishthameha, Haridrameha — these six arise due to pitta. Vasameh, Majjameha, Hastimeha, Madhumeha — these four arise due to vata. These are the twenty types of prameha.

The twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract [yonivyapad] are: Vatiki, Paitiki, Shleshmiki, Sannipatiki — these four, and when associated with contamination by the doshas, sixteen more are described by their particular characteristics — these being: Raktayoni, Arajaska, Acharana, Aticharana, Prakcharana, Upashthata, Udavartini, Kaninee, Sutaghni, Antarmukhi, Suchimukhi, Shushka, Vamini, Shandayoni, Mahayoni — these constitute the twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract. This enumeration is given only as a general teaching, and the relevant verses [shlokas] on this are as follows: The unit of twenty, one triad — these three, two; eight pairs, two; ten, four, two — twelve; five, two; four groups of eight, six groups of three — this eight-type chapter on disease concerning three sets of seven reveals these diseases. ॥ 1 ॥

All disorders whatsoever do not arise from anything other than vata, pitta, and kapha. Just as a bird flying all day long does not transcend its own shadow, so too all disorders arising from the imbalance of one's own bodily constituents [dhatus] cannot be separated from vata, pitta, and kapha. By carefully examining the origin, site, form, nature, characteristics, symptoms, pain, nomenclature, effect, and treatment specific to vata, pitta, and kapha, the wise [physicians] designate all disorders by those very names. ॥ 2 ॥

Here follow the verses [shlokas]:

Disorders arising from the imbalance of one's own bodily constituents [svadhatuvaishamya]...

[Chapter heading:] In the Charaka Samhita

[Left column, verse 3 Sanskrit:]
These [agantuka/exogenous diseases] are present in the body, [yet] are not separate from pitta, kapha, and vata; they are exogenous and thus are distinguished from them. || 3 ||

[Left column, Hindi commentary on verse 3:]
In these two verses it is said that the many groups of disorders which arise due to imbalance of one's own dhatus (bodily tissues) are not, in the body, separate from pitta, kapha, and vata — only the agantuka (exogenous) ones are distinguished from them. || 3 ||

[Left column, verse 4 Sanskrit:]
The exogenous [disease] follows the endogenous disorder, and the greatly aggravated endogenous [disease] follows the exogenous. Having properly understood the association (anubandha) and the constitution (prakriti) in each case, one should then begin treatment. || 4 ||

[Left column, colophon:]
Thus ends, in the work composed by Agnivesha and revised by Charaka, the nineteenth chapter called the Rogachatushka (Group of Four on Disease), in the Ashtaudariya section. || 19 ||

[Left column, Hindi commentary on verse 4:]
The exogenous [disease] follows one's own [endogenous] disorder, and when the endogenous disorder is greatly aggravated, it follows the exogenous. Having well understood the association (samsarga) and the constitution in it, one should then commence treatment. || 4 ||

End of the Rogachatushka Ashtaudariya chapter. || 19 ||

[Left column, chapter heading:]
Chapter Twenty.

Now we shall explain the chapter on Maharoga (great/major diseases).

Thus spoke the venerable Atreya.

Now the description of the Maharoga chapter is given — this is what Bhagavan Atreya says:

[Right column, Sanskrit text:]
Four types of diseases arise: exogenous (agantuka), and those caused by vata, pitta, and kapha. The disease-nature of all four of these is of one kind, due to the commonality of pain. Their constitution (prakriti) is twofold, based on the division into exogenous and endogenous; and this twofold [division] is further specified by whether the seat is mental or physical. The varieties of disorders from these are innumerable, because the specificities of their constitutions, seats, signs, locations, and variations are without number.

The causes of the exogenous disease are: nail-wounds, bites, falling objects, sorcery, curses, physician's mistakes, injuries, bondage, torment, rope-burns, fire-burns, mantras, possession by spirits and beings, and so forth. The cause of the endogenous disease is the imbalance of vata, pitta, and kapha. For both exogenous and endogenous, the causes are: unwholesome conjunction of the senses with their objects, intellectual transgressions (prajnaparadha), and the effect of time (parinama).

All four of these diseases, when greatly aggravated, become mutually connected, yet they do not become confused with one another. For the exogenous [disease], pain arises first and then subsequently produces imbalance of vata, pitta, and kapha. In the endogenous [disease], vata, pitta, and kapha first go into imbalance and then produce pain. Regarding the three doshas — their locations in the body [the text continues on the next page]...

translation:
( 172 )

[Chapter on Diseases — Charaka Samhita]

[Enumeration of Vata disorders continues:] ...convulsive disease, disease of the whole body, hemiplegia, seizures, tetanus-like rigidity, fatigue, giddiness, trembling, yawning, despondency, excessive talking, lassitude, dryness, roughness, dark-reddish discoloration of the skin, sleeplessness, and mental instability — these eighty disorders of Vata. [7]

Now, diseases arise from four causes — Vata, Pitta, Kapha, and external (Agantuja) factors. Among all four types of diseases, the quality of "being a disease" is a single common characteristic. Their nature falls into two divisions: external (Agantuja) and intrinsic (Nija). Their seats are likewise of two kinds, depending on mind or body. Their manifestations are too numerous to count, because the variations of constitution, seat, symptoms, age, and bodily form are countless. The external causes include: scratching by nails, biting, falls, black magic, curses, evil contact, binding, restraint, physical injury, burns by rope or fire, mantras, thunderbolts, spirit-possession, and so on. The intrinsic cause is the imbalance of Vata, Pitta, and Kapha. Both external and intrinsic diseases share the same precipitating factors — improper sensory contact, intellectual errors (Prajnaparadha), and the effects of time. All four types of diseases, when fully aggravated, mutually reinforce one another and cannot be distinguished from each other with certainty. An external disease, once arising as described, causes a subtle imbalance of Vata, Pitta, and Kapha.

In an intrinsic disease, Vata, Pitta, and Kapha first become imbalanced and cause subtle suffering. The sites of these three doshas in the body are as follows: the bladder, the seat of waste, the hips, thighs, feet, and bones are the locations of Vata — and among these, the pakashaya (large intestine) is the special seat of Vata. Sweat, plasma, lymph, blood, and the stomach are the seats of Pitta — and among these, the stomach is the special seat of Pitta. The head, joints, stomach, and fat tissue are the seats of Kapha — and among these, the abdomen is the special seat of Kapha. Vata, Pitta, and Kapha, moving throughout the entire body, when vitiated or un-vitiated, produce favorable or unfavorable effects. In their natural state they produce growth, strength, complexion, clarity, and other good qualities; when they become disordered they produce pathological conditions called vikaras (diseases). These vikaras are of two kinds: Samanyaja (common to the dosha in general) and Nanatmaja (specific to each dosha). The Samanyaja types were described earlier in the chapter on the eight abdominal diseases. The Nanatmaja types are described in this chapter. They are as follows: eighty disorders of Vata, forty disorders of Pitta, and twenty disorders of Kapha. We now describe the disorders of Vata: they are — cracking of nails, cracked heels, pain in the feet, foot-drop, numbness of the feet, lameness due to Vata, stiffness of the ankle, cramps in the calf muscles, sciatica, pain in the knee joints, rigidity of the knees, stiffness of the thighs, exhaustion of the thighs, paralysis, prolapse of the rectum, pain in the rectum, elevation of the testes, rigidity of the penis, inguinal swelling, distension, pain in the sacral region, diarrhea, reverse movement of wind (udavarta), limping, hunchback, dwarfism, pain in the sacrum, [continues on next page]...

Graha (seizure), parshvavamarda (pain in the sides), udara-veshta (abdominal constriction), hridmoh (cardiac stupor), hridrava (palpitation), obstruction in the chest, udharsha (horripilation), bahu-shosha (wasting of the arms), stiffness of the shoulders, stiffness of the neck, constriction of the throat, striking of the jaw, cracking of the lips, splitting of the teeth, looseness, muteness, difficulty of speech, astringent taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth, loss of taste, loss of sense of smell, destruction of smell, earache, hearing of no sound, excessively acute hearing, deafness, rigidity of the back, contraction of the back, dimness of vision, pain in the eyes, dryness of the eyes, burning of the brows, splitting pain at the temples, pain in the forehead, headache, cracking of the hair roots, facial paralysis (ardita), disease of one limb, disease of all limbs, hemiplegia, convulsions, rigidity (dandaka), fatigue, giddiness, trembling, yawning, despondency, excessive talking, languor, roughness, harshness, dark and reddish complexion, sleeplessness, and restlessness — these are the eighty disorders of Vata. (1)

The disorders of Vata are too numerous to count; those described are only the most manifest ones. Among all these Vata disorders — both those described and those not mentioned — the essential nature (atma-rupa) of Vata, which is unchanging, and the characteristic signs of its actions (karma-svalakshana): knowing these, or upon observing even a part of them, skilled physicians without doubt conclude that it is indeed a Vata disorder. (2)

Thus:

Roughness, lightness, coldness of sensation, coolness, movement, and formlessness — these are the inherent qualities (atma-rupa) of Vata. Because of this very nature, the characteristic signs of its actions are also of this kind. When Vata enters each particular part of the body, the following occur: dislocation, displacement, distension, breaking of body parts, languor, excitement, thirst, convolution, grinding pain, trembling, movement, pricking pain, piercing pain, constriction, breaking — and likewise roughness, harshness, clearness, porousness, redness, astringency, tastelessness, dryness, colic pain, loss of memory, contraction, stiffness — these are the actions of Vata. Upon seeing a person afflicted with these, one should conclude with certainty that it is a Vata disorder. (3)

translation:
( 174 )

[The treatment of vata disorders should be undertaken] with sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, and warm measures. Fomentation (sveda), oleation (sneha), asthapana (enema), anuvasan (oil enema), nasal therapies (nasya), dietary measures, massage (abhyanga), stimulating treatments (utsadana), bathing/sprinkling (parisheka), and other vata-alleviating measures should be applied in proper measure and at the proper time. Physicians consider asthapana and anuvasan to be the most important of all treatments for vata disorders. || 4 ||

Once that medicine enters the digestive organ (pakashaya) first, it severs only the pathological root of vata. Even when vata has not been fully subdued, the vata disorders residing within the body are brought to pacification — just as when the root of a plant is cut, the trunk, branches, aerial roots, flowers, fruits, leaves, and so on are all inevitably destroyed. || 5 ||

[Hindi commentary:] From the beginning, that medicine, entering the digestive organ, cuts only the pathological root of vata. And when the vata disorder is destroyed, all vata disorders residing within the body attain pacification — just as when the root of a plant is cut, the trunk, branches, off-shoots, flowers, fruits, and so on are inevitably destroyed. || 5 ||

Now forty disorders of pitta will be described. They are as follows: burning sensation (osha), extreme burning (purosa), daha (burning), davahu (scorching), dhumaka (smoky sensation), amlaka (sour eructation), vidaha (burning indigestion), antardaha (internal burning), amsadaha (burning of the shoulders), excess body heat (ushmadhikya), excessive sweating and body odor (atisveda and anga-gandha), cracking of body parts (angavayava-darana), moistening/putrefaction of blood (shonita-kleda), putrefaction of muscle (mamsa-kleda), burning of skin (tvag-daha), burning of muscle (mamsa-daha), cracking of skin and muscle (tvang-mamsa-darana), cracking of the dermis (charma-darana), urticarial rash (rakta-kotha), blood blisters (rakta-visphota), rakta-pitta (bleeding disorder), red patches (rakta-mandala), greenish discoloration (hiratva), yellowish discoloration (haridratva), bluish patches (nilika), skin eruptions (kasha), jaundice (kamala), bitter taste in the mouth (tikta-asyata), putrid mouth smell (putimukha), excessive thirst (trishna-adhikhya), non-satisfaction (atripti), ulceration of the mouth (asya-paka), ulceration of the throat (gala-paka), ulceration of the eyes (akshi-paka), ulceration of the rectum (guda-paka), ulceration of the penis (medhra-paka), delirium (jivadana), blackouts (tamah-pravesha), and greenish-yellow discoloration of urine, eyes, and skin — thus these forty disorders of pitta. Of the pitta disorders, further [the text continues on the next page]...

सूत्रस्थानम् । ( १७५ )

संख्येयानामाविष्कृततमाभ्याख्याताभवन्ति ॥ ६ ॥

तैसेही पित्तके चालीस विकार इससे आगे वर्णन करतेहैं वे ऐसे हैं कि छेभ–दाह–क्षवथु–धूमक–अम्लक विदाह–अन्तर्दाह–अंशदाह–ऊष्माकी अधिकता– अतिस्वेद– अंगागंध–अङ्गावयव कारण, शोणित, क्षेद, मांसक्षेद–त्वचाका दाह–मांस दाह–त्वचा और मांसका– दरण–चर्मका दरण–रक्तकी–रक्तविस्फोट–रक्तपित्त–रक्तमण्डल–हारितता–हारिद्रत्व–नीलीका कक्षा– कामला– तिक्तमुख–मुखमें दुर्गन्ध–तृष्णाकी अधिकता अत्यंत मुखका पाक–गलपाक अक्षिपाक–गुरुपाक–लिङ्गपाक– जीवादान– तमकाप्रवेश हरित हलदीके समान नेत्र मूत्र मल इनका होना, ये चालीस–पित्तके विकारहैं असंख्य पित विकारोंके मध्यमें जो प्रकटहैं वे वर्णन कियेहैं ॥ ६ ॥

सर्वेष्वपिखल्वेतेषुपित्तविकारेष्वन्येषुचानुक्तेषुपित्तस्येदमात्मरूपमपरिणामिकर्मणश्वस्वलक्षणंयत्दुपलभ्यतद्वयवंवाविमुक्तसन्देहाः पित्तविकारमेवाध्यवस्यन्तिकुशलाः ॥ ७ ॥

संपूर्णभी इन पित्तोंके विकारोंमें और अन्योंमें पित्तका यह अपरिणामी आत्मरूप– और कर्मका– स्वलक्षण रहताहै– जिसको उसके अवयवकी–जानकर–

संदेह रहित कुशल वैद्य–पित विकार–काही निश्चय करतेहैं ॥ ७ ॥

तथथा ।

औष्ण्यंतैक्ष्ण्यंलाघवमनितस्नेहो वर्णश्चशुक्लारुणवर्जोगन्धश्चविस्रो रसौचकटुकाम्लौपित्तस्यात्मरूपाणि । एवंविधत्वाचकर्मणःस्वलक्षणिमदमस्यभवति । तंतंशरीरावयवमाविशतोदाहोष्मपाकस्वेदक्षेदकोथस्नावरागाःयथास्वञ्ग न्धवर्णरसादिभिर्निर्वर्तनंपित्तस्य कर्मिणितैरन्वितंपित्तविकारमेवाध्यवसेयत् ॥ ८ ॥

वह ऐसे हैं कि उष्णता–तीक्षणता–लघुता अत्यन्त–स्नेहका अभाव–शुक्ल–रक्तसे भिन्न–वर्ण–और विस्रगंध कटुक अम्ल–रसहों–ये पित्तके आत्मरूप हैं–इस प्रकार–कर्मके होनेपर–यह पित्तका स्वलक्षण होताहै–कि तिस तिस शरीरके अवयवमें–प्रविष्ट हुए पित्तसे दाह–ऊष्मा पाक–स्वेद–क्षेद–कोथ–कण्डू स्नाव–राग और यथायोग्य–गन्धवर्ण–रसोंका होना ये पित्त–के कर्म हैं इनके सम्बन्यसे–पित विकार काही निश्चय करे ॥ ८ ॥

तंमधुरतिक्तकषायशीतैरुपक्रमैरुपक्रमेतस्नेहिविरेकभेदहपरिषेकाभ्यङ्गावगाहादिभिःपित्तहरैर्मात्रां
translation:
Sutra Sthana (Chapter on Fundamental Principles), Page 175

The most manifest among the enumerable ones are thus described. (Verse 6)

In the same way, the forty disorders of pitta are described hereafter. They are as follows: burning sensation (chha), scorching heat (daha), sneezing (kshvathu), smoky sensation (dhumaka), hyperacidity (amlaka), internal burning (antardaha), partial burning (anshadaha), excess of heat, excessive sweating, body odor, reasons relating to the limbs, bleeding (shonita), moistness (ksheda), muscular erosion (mamsaksheda), burning of the skin, burning of the flesh, tearing of the skin and flesh, tearing of the dermis, hemorrhagic conditions, hemorrhagic spots, hemorrhagic rash, yellowish-green discoloration, yellow discoloration, bluish discoloration, jaundice (kamala), bitter taste in the mouth, foul smell in the mouth, excess thirst, stomatitis, inflammation of the throat, inflammation of the eyes, inflammation of the large intestine, inflammation of the genitals, fainting, coma, and the occurrence of urine, stool, and eyes resembling the color of green turmeric — these are the forty disorders of pitta. Among the countless pitta disorders, those that are most manifest have been described. (Verse 6)

In all these pitta disorders, and in others not mentioned here, the essential nature of pitta — its unchanging inherent form and the characteristic signs of its action — when perceived, allow skilled physicians to determine without doubt that it is indeed a pitta disorder. (Verse 7)

In all these pitta disorders and others, the unchanging inherent nature of pitta and the characteristic signs of its actions remain constant. A skilled physician who recognizes these characteristics in the constituents of a patient can diagnose a pitta disorder without doubt. (Verse 7)

Thus:

Heat, sharpness, lightness, slight unctuousness, a color other than white and red, a fetid odor, and pungent and sour tastes — these are the essential characteristics of pitta. Accordingly, the characteristic signs of its action are as follows: when pitta enters the various parts of the body, it produces burning, heat, suppuration, sweating, softening, putrefaction, itching, secretion, and redness, along with appropriate odor, color, and taste. These are the functions of pitta. Based on these associated signs, one should diagnose pitta disorders. (Verse 8)

Treatment should be undertaken with sweet, bitter, astringent, and cooling therapies, along with unctuous purgation, enemas, pouring of liquids (parisheka), anointing (abhyanga), immersion baths (avagaha), and other pitta-pacifying measures in appropriate doses...

न्तेभिषजः ॥ ९ ॥

translation:
( 176 )

One should measure by time and proper quantity. Purgation is regarded by physicians as the most important of all therapeutic measures specifically for disorders dominated by pitta. (9)

Using sweet, bitter, astringent, and cooling treatments — with snehana (oleation), virechana (purgation), pradeha (poultice), parisheka (sprinkling), abhyanga (massage), and other pitta-reducing substances, administered in the correct measure and at the correct time — purgation is considered by physicians to be supreme above all treatments for pitta disorders. (9)

That (pitta), entering from the very origin into the stomach, destroys the root of the aberrant pitta alone; and when the pitta situated within the body is thus subdued, the pitta-disorders throughout the body attain resolution — just as when fire is removed, the fireplace alone becomes cold. (10)

That (treatment), having entered the stomach from the very source, destroys the root of the pitta disorder. When pitta is destroyed in the stomach, the pitta-disorders within the body come to peace in the same manner — just as when fire is extinguished, the hearth alone becomes cold. (10)

Now twenty disorders of kapha (phlegm) will be described. They are as follows: satiety, drowsiness, excessive sleep, heaviness of the body, stiffness, laziness, sweet taste in the mouth, salivation, belching, expulsion of phlegm, excessive stool, coating of the throat, valasa (a disease), coating over the heart, thickening of the blood vessels, goiter, excessive obesity, cold digestive fire, urticaria (udarda), whitish appearance, and whiteness of urine, eyes, and feces — these twenty are the disorders of kapha. (11)

The twenty disorders of kapha are as follows: satiety, drowsiness, excessive sleep, heaviness of body, stiffness, laziness, sweetness in the mouth, salivation, belching, expectoration of phlegm, excessive stool, coating of the throat, valasa, coating of the heart, increase (thickening) of blood vessels, goiter, extreme obesity, cold digestive fire, urticaria, whitish complexion, and whiteness of urine, eyes, and feces — these are the twenty disorders of kapha. (11)

Those disorders of kapha that are beyond complete enumeration have been described — only the most prominent among them. In all of these disorders of kapha, and in other unmentioned ones as well, when the characteristic nature of kapha and the signs of its transformative action are observed — whether completely or partially — skilled physicians confidently classify it as a kapha disorder. (12)

Among the innumerable disorders of kapha, those that are most clearly manifest have been described here —

सूत्रस्थानम्
( १७७ )

संपूर्णे इन कफके विकारोंमें और अन्य
जो नहीं कहेहैं उनमें कफका यह अप-
रिणामि अपना रूप और कर्मका स्वल
क्षण जो वह मिलै वा उसका अवयव

विकारही निश्चय करतेहैं ॥ १२ ॥

तद्यथा–श्वैत्यशैत्यगौरवमाधुर्य्य
मात्स्य्यांिणश्लेष्मणआत्मरूपा
ण्येवंविधत्वाचकर्मणःस्वलक्षण
मिदमस्यभवति । तंतंशरीरावय
वमाविशतः श्वैत्यशैत्यकण्डूस्थै
र्य्यंगौरवस्नेहस्तम्भसुतिक्लेदोपदेह
बन्धमाधुर्य्यिचिरकारित्वानिश्ले
ष्मणःकर्माणितैरन्वितंश्लेष्मिव
कारमेवाध्यवस्येत् ॥ १३ ॥

वह ऐसेहैं कि स्नेह शीत शुक्लता
गौरव मधुरता मंदता ये कफके आत्म
रूपहैं इसी प्रकारका होनेसे कर्मका
स्वलक्षण यही होताहै तिस २ शरीरके
अवयवमें प्रविष्ट होते हुये कफके श्वेत
शीत कंडु स्थिरता गौरव स्नेह स्तंभ
सुति क्लेद उपदेह बंध माधुर्य चिर
कारी ये कर्म होतेहैं उनसे युक्त रोगमें
कफके विकारकाही निश्चय करतेहैं॥१३

तंकटुकितक्ककषायतीक्ष्णोष्णरू
क्षैरुपक्रमैरुपक्रमेतस्वेदनवमनशि
रोविरेचनव्यायामादिभिःश्लेष्म

हरैर्मांत्रांकालञ्चप्रमाणीकृत्य ।
वमनन्तुसर्वोपक्रमेत्यःश्लेष्मिणञ्च
धानतमंमन्यन्तेभिषजः ॥ १४ ॥

उसकी कटु तिक्त कषाय तीक्ष्ण उष्ण
रूक्ष इन उपक्रमोंसे चिकित्साकरै–स्वेद
वमन शिरका विरेचन व्यायाम आदि
जो कफहारीहैं उनसे मात्रा कालके
प्रमाणसे करै–संपूर्ण उप क्रमोंसे वम-
नको तो वैद्य अत्यंत प्रधान कफमें
मानतेहैं ॥ १४ ॥

तञ्च्यादितएवामाशयमनुप्रविश्य
केवलंवैकारिकंश्लेष्ममूलमपकर्ष
ति । तत्राविजतेश्लेष्मण्यपिशरी
रान्तगताःश्लष्मिवकाराःप्रशा
न्तिमापध्यन्ते । यथाभिन्नेकेदा
रसेतौशालियवषष्टिकादीन्यिभ
ष्यन्यमानानिनअभ्सामशोषमा
पध्यन्तेतद्दिदिति ॥ १५ ॥

वह आदिसे ही आमाशयमें प्रविष्ट
होकर केवल विकारकेही कफके
मूलको नष्ट करताहै उसमें छेष्मके
नष्ट होनेपर शरीरके अंतर्गत कफके
विकार ऐसे शांतिको प्राप्त होतेहैं जैसे
केदार ( खेत ) के सेतुके भेद होनेपर

भवन्तिचात्र ।
रोगमादौपरीक्षेततोऽनन्तरमौष

१२
translation:
Sutra Sthana
(177)

In all the disorders of kapha described above, and in others not specifically mentioned, when the physician finds the intrinsic nature and characteristic signs of kapha — or its components — present, he should diagnose the condition as a kapha disorder without hesitation. (12)

These intrinsic characteristics are: whiteness, coldness, heaviness, sweetness — these are the essential qualities of kapha. Correspondingly, the characteristic signs of its action are as follows. When kapha enters each bodily part, the symptoms are: whiteness, coldness, itching, firmness, heaviness, unctuousness, stiffness, secretion, moistening, coating, binding, sweetness, and slow action. When a disease is associated with these symptoms, the physician should conclude it is definitely a kapha disorder. (13)

One should treat such a condition with remedies that are pungent, bitter, astringent, sharp, hot, and dry — using therapies such as sudation (sweating), emesis (vomiting), head-purging, exercise, and similar measures that reduce kapha —

— administering them in the proper dose and at the proper time. Among all these therapeutic measures, emesis is considered by physicians to be the foremost remedy in predominant kapha conditions. (14)

Such emesis, entering first into the stomach, uproots the very source of the pathological kapha alone. When the kapha there is defeated, the kapha disorders elsewhere throughout the body also attain relief — just as, when the embankment of an irrigated field is breached, the rice, barley, and shashtika grain and similar crops, having received water, then dry up as the water drains away. (15)

And on this topic, the following verses are cited:
One should first examine the disease, then thereafter the medicine —

translation:
( 178 )
In the Charaka Samhita.

[Verse 16:] ...thereafter the physician-practitioner should act with prior knowledge. This verse states: first examine the disease, then the medicine, then the procedure, and then the physician should treat with full knowledge. (16)

[Verse 17:] A physician who undertakes treatment without properly understanding the disease — even if he knows the rules of medicines — his success comes only by chance. That is, it may happen or it may not. (17)

[Verse 18:] But one who knows the specific nature of the disease, who is versed in all medical procedures, and who knows the measures appropriate to place and time — his success is without doubt. (18)

Summary verses of this section:
[Verse 19:] Collection, constitution, locality, the presenting form of the disorder, its prompting cause, freedom from doubt, and its associated conditions — all these have been described with respect to diseases. (19)

[Verse 20:] The sites of the doshas, the groups of diseases, the many ways in which they arise, the distinct forms of each dosha separately, and whatever their actions that do not undergo transformation — (20)

[Verse 21:] The separate treatment-approaches for the doshas have been prescribed; the one who perceives the truth — Punarvasu — has well described them in the chapter on great diseases, for the proper welfare of the diseased. (21)

Thus ends, in the Rogachatushka composed by Agnivesha and redacted by Charaka, the chapter called Maharogadhyaya, the twentieth chapter. The Rogachatushka is concluded.

Twenty-First Chapter.
Now we shall explain the chapter called Ashtauninditiya (the eight censured types of persons). So says the revered Atreya.

After this, the description of the Ashtauninditiya chapter is given — this is what the revered Atreya declares.

In this world, with reference to the body, eight types of persons are considered censured. They are as follows: the excessively tall, the excessively short, the excessively hairy...

translation:

...nor extremely dark-complexioned, nor extremely fair, nor extremely obese, nor extremely emaciated. (1)

What is established here, regarding the subject of the body, is that eight types of persons are condemned: those who are excessively tall, excessively short, excessively hairy, hairless, extremely dark, extremely fair, extremely obese, or extremely emaciated. (5)

Among these, the extremely obese and the extremely emaciated have further specific faults. For the extremely obese, the following eight faults arise: shortening of lifespan, obstruction of aging (i.e., premature degeneration), difficulty in sexual activity, weakness, foul odor, excessive sweating, excessive hunger, and excessive thirst. (2)

Such excessive obesity arises from overeating, from habitual use of heavy, sweet, cold, and unctuous foods, from lack of exercise, from abstinence from sexual activity, from sleeping during the day and seeking constant comfort, from freedom from anxiety, and from the natural constitution of one's seed (heredity). (3)

That obesity arises from excessive fullness, and from habitual use of heavy, sweet, cold, and unctuous substances, from lack of exercise, from abstaining from intercourse, from sleeping during the day and seeking pleasure habitually, from freedom from worry, and from the nature of one's constitution. (3)

In one who is excessively fat, only fat continues to increase while the other bodily tissues do not grow accordingly. Therefore, his lifespan is shortened. Because of laxity and delicacy combined with the heaviness of fat, the normal process of aging is obstructed. Because of the abundance of semen being blocked by fat obstructing the passages, sexual activity becomes difficult. Weakness arises from the imbalance of the bodily tissues. Foul odor comes from the fault of fat itself and from its tendency to produce sweat. Because of the association with phlegm and excessive discharge, there is excessive sweating. Because of the sharpness of the digestive fire in the abdomen and the nature of the bodily wind, excessive hunger and excessive thirst arise. (4)

In the body of one who is extremely fat, fat alone increases while the other tissues do not grow correspondingly. Hence there is a diminution (lessening) of his vitality. Due to laxity, delicacy, and the heaviness of fat, the process of aging is obstructed. Because the pathways are blocked by fat and semen is not properly formed, sexual activity is difficult. Weakness arises from the imbalance of the tissues. Due to the faulty nature of fat and its tendency to produce sweat, foul odor results. Because of the association of fat with phlegm and increased discharge, and because exercise cannot be tolerated...

translation:
( 180 )

Causing excessive perspiration and, due to intense digestive fire, expansion of wind in the gut, leading to extreme hunger and extreme thirst — thus it is. (4)

And on this subject [the following verses apply]:

"Because the channels are obstructed by fat, the wind moving especially within the gut kindles the digestive fire and also dries up the food." (5)

This verse says that because the channels are blocked by fat, the wind circulating especially in the gut intensifies the digestive fire and also desiccates the food. (5)

"Therefore it quickly produces a craving for food, and after a short while one suffers terrible disorders." (6)

Thus it quickly produces hunger and desire for food, and after some time one experiences severe disorders. (6)

"These two — fire and wind — are particularly the causes of affliction. They burn the obese person just as a forest fire burns a forest." (7)

These two, fire and wind, are especially the causative agents of disturbance; they consume the obese person in the same way that a forest fire consumes a forest. (7)

"When fat increases excessively, the winds along with [other humors] swiftly produce terrible disorders and quickly destroy life." (8)

When fat increases excessively, the wind and others quickly produce severe disorders and destroy life. (8)

"Due to extreme increase of fat and flesh, the buttocks, abdomen, and breasts sway and hang; one who has growth without proper vigor is called extremely obese." (9)

When fat and flesh grow excessively, the buttocks, abdomen, and breasts become pendulous and swaying; one whose increase of bulk brings no corresponding vitality is called extremely obese. (9)

"Thus the faults, causes, and manifestations of the obese person have been described; what is to be said next regarding excessive emaciation will now be stated." (10)

The faults, causes, and signs of obesity have been described; what needs to be said about extreme emaciation will now be explained. (10)

"Use of dry foods and drinks, fasting, limited eating, excessive physical activity, grief, suppression of sleep and natural urges —" (11)

Consumption of rough dry food and liquids, fasting, restricted diet, excessive exertion, sorrow, and suppression of sleep and natural urges — (11)

"Habitual use of dry unctions, bathing, natural constitution, old age, lingering after-effects of disease, and anger — all these produce an excessively emaciated person." (12)

सब मनुष्योंको अत्यंतकुश करतेहैं॥ १२॥

व्यायाममितिसौहित्यंक्षुतिपासा
मथौषधम्। क्षोनसहतेतद्दति
शीतोष्णमैथुनम् ॥ १३ ॥

व्यायाम अत्यंत हृति क्षुधा पिपासा
मद शीत उष्ण मैथुन इनको कुश मनुष्य
नहीं सह सकता ॥ १३ ॥

प्लीहाकासःक्षयःश्वासोगुल्माशाँ
स्युदराणिच । कशंप्रायोऽभिभा
वन्तिरोगाश्चग्रहणीगताः ॥ १४॥

प्लीहा कास क्षय श्वास गुल्म अशँ
उदरके रोग और ग्रहणीके रोग ये सब
कुश मनुष्यमें दौडतेहैं ॥ १४ ॥

शुष्कस्फगुदरग्रीवोधमनीजालस
न्ततः। त्वगस्थिशोषोऽतिकुशः
स्थूपलवनिरोमतः ॥ १५ ॥

स्फक् ( नितंब ) उदर ग्रीवा ये
जिसके शुष्क हों धमनीयोंके जालका
विस्तार हो त्वचा अस्थि शेष हों–पर्वस्थूल
हों वह नर अत्यंत कुश कहाताहै॥ १५॥

सततव्याधितावेताविस्थूलक
शौनरौ । सततंचोपचर्यौहिक
ष्णैर्वृंहणैरपि ॥ १६ ॥

ये अतिस्थूल अतिकुश मनुष्य–निरं-
तर व्याधित रहतेहैं और कर्षण और
वृंहणसे निरंतर उपचार करने योग्यहैं॥ १६

स्थैल्यकार्श्यंवरकार्श्यंसमोपकर
णौहितौ । यथुभौष्याधिरागञ्छे
त्स्थूलमेवातिपीडयेत् ॥ १७॥

स्थूलता और कुशतामें कुशता
अच्छीहै क्योंकि समानहै उपकरण जिनके
ऐसे उन दोनोंको व्याधि आवे तो स्थूल-
कोही अत्यंत पीडा देतीहै ॥ १७ ॥

सममांसप्रमाणस्तुसमसंहननोन
रः । इंद्देन्द्रयत्वाद्व्याधीनांनब
लेनाभिभूयते ॥ १८ ॥

जिस मनुष्यके मांसका प्रमाण समा-
नहै और संहनन ( देहकी बनावट ) भी
समान हो और इंद्रियोंकी दृढता होनेसे
उस मनुष्यको व्याधि बलसे नहीं दबा
सकती ॥ १८ ॥

क्षुतिपासातपसहःशीतव्यायाम
संसहः। सयपक्कासमजरःसममां
सचयोमतः ॥ १९ ॥

क्षुधा पिपासा आतप इनको सहसके
शीतल व्यायाम इनका संयह करे–सम-
पाक हो समजरा हो सम मांसका समूह
उस पूर्वोक्त नरमें होताहै ॥ १९ ॥

गुरुचातपंणचेऽंस्थूलानांकर्षणंम
ति। कशानांबृंहणार्थेचलघुसन्त
पणञयत् ॥ २० ॥

स्थूल मनुष्योंके कर्षणके लिये गुरु
अपतर्पण इष्टहै और कुश मनुष्योंकी
वृद्धिके लिये लघु जो संतर्पण वह इष्टहै२०

translation:
Sutra Sthana
(Page 182)

Dry rubbing (udvartana), bathing practices, natural aging and its disorders, anger — all these make human beings extremely emaciated. [12]

Exercise, overeating, hunger, thirst, emetic medicines — a lean person cannot endure these along with cold, heat, and sexual activity. [13]

Diseases of the spleen, cough, consumption, asthma, abdominal tumors (gulma), piles, diseases of the abdomen, and diseases of the intestines — all these tend to overwhelm the lean person. [14]

One whose buttocks, abdomen, and neck are dried up, whose network of veins is prominent, whose body is reduced to skin and bone, and whose joints are enlarged, is called an extremely emaciated person. [15]

These two — the excessively obese and the excessively emaciated — are constantly afflicted by disease and constantly require treatment: the obese with reducing (karshana) therapies and the emaciated with nourishing (brimhana) therapies. [16]

Between obesity and leanness, leanness is preferable, because when disease strikes both types equally, it is the obese person who suffers the most intense affliction. [17]

A person whose flesh is of proper measure and whose physical constitution is also balanced, and who possesses steady sense organs, cannot be overpowered by diseases by force. [18]

One who can endure hunger, thirst, and heat, who can tolerate cold and exercise, who digests food evenly, ages evenly, and has an even accumulation of flesh — such a person is described as ideal. [19]

For the reduction of obese persons, heavy non-nourishing (apatarpana) therapy is recommended; and for the growth of the emaciated, a light nourishing (santarpana) therapy is prescribed. [20]

text:
( १८२ )
Digitized By Siddhi Vinayak Gyaan Kosha
चरकसंहितायाम्

वातघ्नान्यन्नपानानिश्लेष्ममेदोह
राणिच।रूक्षोष्णावस्तयस्तीक्ष्णा
रूक्षाण्युद्वर्तनानिनच ॥ २१ ॥
और वातनाशक अन्नपान और कफ-
मेदाके नाशक और रूक्ष उष्ण बस्ति
रूक्ष उद्वर्तन ॥ २१ ॥

गुडूचीभद्रमुस्तानांप्रयोगस्त्रैफल
स्तथा । तक्कारिष्टप्रयोगस्तुप्रयो
गोमाक्षिकस्यच ॥ २२ ॥
गिलोह भद्र ( कदंब ) मोथा इनका
और त्रिफलाका प्रयोग मठा और
मदिराका प्रयोग-शहतका प्रयोग ॥२२॥

विडङ्गनागरंक्षारःकाललोहरजोम
धु । यवामलकचूर्णञ्चप्रयोगःश्रेष्ठ
उच्यते ॥ २३ ॥
बायविडंग सोंठ क्षार–कंकोल-लोहे-
की भस्म मधु ( शहत ) जौ आंवले
इनका चूर्ण मिलाकर–श्रेष्ठ प्रयोग कहा
है ॥ २३ ॥

बिल्वादिपञ्चमूलस्यप्रयोगःक्षौद्र
संयुतः । शिलाजतुप्रयोगस्तुसा
बिमन्थरसाशिला ॥ २४ ॥
बेल आदि पांच मूलका जो शहतसे
युक्त प्रयोग है और अग्निमंथ ( अरणी )
के रस सहित सिलाजीतका प्रयोग
उत्तम है ॥ २४ ॥

प्रसातिकाप्रियंगुश्श्यामाकायव

कायवाः । जूर्णाढ्याःकोद्रवामुद्गा
कुलत्थाश्चक्रमर्दकाः ॥ २५ ॥
प्रसातिका ( निवार ) प्रियंगु (राई)
श्यामाक यवक, यव, जूर्णहू ( जुवार )
कोदों मूंग कुलथीचक्रमुद्रके ( मूंगके
भले ) ॥ २५ ॥

आढकीनाञ्चबीजानिपटोलाम
लकैःसह । भोजनार्थेप्रयोज्यानि
पानञ्चानुमधूदकम् ॥ २६ ॥
आढकी ( अरहर ) के बीज पटोल
आंवले ये भोजनके लिये देना और
मधूदकका अनुपान देना ॥ २६ ॥

अरिष्टांश्चानुपानार्थेमेदोमांसक
फापहाचू। अतिस्थौल्यविनाशा
यसंविभज्यप्रयोजयेत् ॥ २७ ॥
और अरिष्ट ( नोंब ) को और मेदां
मांस कफ इनके नाशकोंको, अनुपानके
अर्थ पृथक् २ करके अति स्थूलताके
विनाशक लिये दे ॥ २७ ॥

प्रजागरंव्यवायञ्चव्यायामंचिन्त
नानिच । स्थौल्यमिच्छन्परि
त्यजेत्क्रमेणाभिप्रवर्धयेत्॥ २८ ॥
अति जागरण व्यवाय व्यायाम
चिंता इनको स्थूलताके त्यागका अभि-
लाषी क्रमसे बढावे ॥ २८ ॥

स्वमोहर्षःसुखाशड्यामनसोनिवृ
तिःशमः । चिन्ताव्यवायव्या
यामिवरामःप्रियदर्शनम् ॥ २९ ॥

translation:
(182)
Charaka Samhita

[Verse 21]
Foods and drinks that destroy vata, that remove excess phlegm and fat, that are dry and hot — such enemas (basti) and dry unctions (udvartana) — these are [recommended].
[Commentary 21]: Foods and drinks that destroy vata, and that destroy phlegm and fat, and dry hot enemas and dry unction — these are [prescribed].

[Verse 22]
The use of guduchi (giloy), bhadramusta (kadamba), and nagarmotha (musta); likewise the use of triphala; the use of takka-arishta (buttermilk preparation); and the use of honey — these are [recommended].
[Commentary 22]: Giloy, bhadra (kadamba), motha — their use; and the use of triphala; the use of buttermilk and wine; the use of honey — these are [recommended].

[Verse 23]
Vidanga (embelia), dried ginger, alkali (kshara), black iron powder, honey, barley, and amla (Indian gooseberry) — mixing these into a powder is called the best application.
[Commentary 23]: Vidanga, dried ginger, kshara, kankola, iron ash, honey, barley, and amla — mixing these powders together is declared the best application.

[Verse 24]
The use of the bilva-group of five roots combined with honey, and the use of shilajatu (mineral pitch) together with the juice of agnimantha (shami/arni) — this is excellent.
[Commentary 24]: The use of the five roots beginning with bilva, combined with honey, and the use of shilajatu together with the juice of agnimantha (arni) — this is excellent.

[Verse 25]
Prasatika (nivara rice), priyangु (mustard/raई), shyamaka (a type of millet), small barley, barley, jowar (sorghum), kodrava (kodo millet), mudga (green gram), kulatha (horse gram), and chakramardaka (cassia) — these grains are enriched and [recommended].
[Commentary 25]: Nivara rice, rai (mustard), shyamaka, small barley, barley, jowar, kodo millet, green gram, horse gram, chakramurdaka (a type of green gram) — these are beneficial.

[Verse 26]
The seeds of aadhaки (pigeon pea/arhar), patola (pointed gourd), and amalaki (amla/gooseberry) — these should be used as food, and medicated honey-water should be taken as an accompaniment.
[Commentary 26]: The seeds of arhar (pigeon pea), patola, and amla — give these as food, and give honey-water as an accompanying drink.

[Verse 27]
Arishtas (fermented herbal preparations) should be used as accompaniments, to destroy excess fat, flesh, and phlegm. For the elimination of extreme obesity, they should be prescribed separately according to the case.
[Commentary 27]: Arishta (fermented preparation) and the destroyers of excess fat, flesh, and phlegm — give these separately as accompaniments for the destruction of extreme obesity.

[Verse 28]
Excessive wakefulness, sexual activity, physical exercise, and anxiety — one who wishes to be rid of obesity should gradually increase these.
[Commentary 28]: Excessive wakefulness, sexual activity, physical exercise, and worry — one who desires to reduce obesity should gradually increase these.

[Verse 29]
Self-contentment, happiness of mind, mental peace and calm, the cessation of worry, sexual activity, and exercise, and the sight of pleasant things —

text:
Digitized By Sloपुअस्थानम् Gyaan Kosha ( १८३ )

स्वप्न–हर्ष सुखकी शय्या मनकी
निवृत्ति ( संतोष ) शांति–चिंता व्यवाय
व्यायाम इन तीनोंका विराम–प्रिय वस्तु-
ओंका दर्शन ॥ २९ ॥

नवान्नानिनवंमद्यंग्राम्यानूपौदका
रसाः । संस्कृतानिचमांसानिदिध
सर्पिःपयांसिच ॥ ३० ॥

नवीन अन्न और मद्य ग्रामके रसीले
जल–संस्कृत किये मांस दिध घी दूध ३०

इक्षवःशाल्योमांसागोधूमागुडवै
कृतम् । बस्तयःस्निग्धमधुरास्तै
लाभ्यङ्गश्चसर्वदा ॥ ३१ ॥

इक्षु शालि मांस गोधूम गुडके विकार
स्निग्ध और मधुर बस्ति सर्वदा तैलका
अभ्यंग ॥ ३१ ॥

स्निग्धमुद्वर्तनंस्नानंगन्धमाल्यनिषे
वणम् । शुक्लोवासोयथाकालंदो
षाणामवसेचनम् ॥ ३२ ॥

स्निग्ध उद्वर्तन–स्नान–गंध माल्यका
सेवन शुक्ल वस्त्र और यथाकाल दोषोंका
अवसेचन ॥ ३२ ॥

रसायनानांवृष्याणांयोगानामुपसे
वनम् । हत्वातिकार्श्यमादत्तेनू
णामुपचयंपरम् ॥ ३३ ॥

और रसायन और वृष्य पदार्थोंके
योगोंका सेवन इन सबका प्रयोग–अत्यंत
कृशताको नष्ट करके मनुष्योंकी उत्तम
पुष्टिको करताहै ॥ ३३ ॥

अचिन्तनाचकाभ्याणांभ्रुवंसन्त
पणेनच । स्वमप्रसङ्गाचनरोवरा
हइवपुष्यति ॥ ३४ ॥

और अचिंतन कायोंके अकस्मात्
तर्पणसे और स्वप्नके प्रसंगसे मनुष्य–
वराहके समान पुष्ट होताहै ॥ ३४ ॥

यदातुमनसिक्लान्तेकर्मात्मानःकु
मान्विताः । विषयेभ्योनिवर्तन्ते
तदास्वपितिमानवः ॥ ३५ ॥

जब मन ग्लानिमें होताहै तब ग्लानिसे
युक्त कर्मात्मा ( जीव ) विषयोंसे निवृत्त
होतेहैं तब मनुष्य सोताहै ॥ ३५ ॥

निद्रायतंसुखंदुःखंपुष्टिःकार्श्यंव
लाबलम् । वृषताक्लीबताज्ञानम
ज्ञानंजीवितंनच ॥ ३६ ॥

सुख–दुःख–पुष्टि–कृशता–बल–अबल
वृषता–क्लीबता–ज्ञान–अज्ञान–और जी-
वित ये सब निद्राके अधीनहैं ॥ ३६ ॥

अकालेऽतिप्रसङ्गाचनचनिद्रानि
षेविता । सुखायुषीपराकुभ्यांत्कालरात्रिरवापरा ॥ ३७ ॥

अकालमें और अतिप्रसंगसे–सेवन–
नकीहुई निद्रा उत्तम सुख और अवस्थाको
दूसरी कालरात्रिके समान नहीं करतीहै ३७

सेवयुक्तापुनर्युङ्केनिद्रादेहंसुखा
युषा । पुरुषंयोगिनंसिद्ध्यासत्या
बुद्धिरिवागता ॥ ३८ ॥
translation:
(Page 183 — Susruthasthana, from Charaka Samhita)

Verse 29: Happiness, pleasant bed, mental contentment (satisfaction), peace, cessation of worry, physical exercise, cessation of all three of these, and the sight of beloved objects — these are the causes of sleep.

Verse 30: Fresh grains, new wine, the juices of village and aquatic animals, prepared meats, curds, ghee, and milk — these promote nourishment.

Verse 31: Products made from sugarcane, rice, meat, wheat, and molasses; unctuous and sweet enemas; and daily oil massage — these are always beneficial.

Verse 32: Unctuous massage (udvartana), bathing, use of fragrant substances and garlands, wearing white clothing, and timely elimination of the doshas — these are recommended.

Verse 33: The regular use of rasayanas (rejuvenating formulations) and aphrodisiac substances destroys extreme emaciation and brings the highest level of nourishment to human beings.

Verse 34: Through the sudden and unexpected gratification of desires, through freedom from anxiety, and through indulgence in sleep, a person becomes nourished just like a boar.

Verse 35: When the mind becomes fatigued and the karma-laden soul (jiva), afflicted by weariness, withdraws from sense-objects, then a person falls asleep.

Verse 36: Happiness and sorrow, nourishment and emaciation, strength and weakness, virility and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, and life itself — all these depend upon sleep.

Verse 37: Sleep that is taken at the wrong time or in excess does not bring good health and long life; rather, it is like another night of death (kalaratri).

Verse 38: But sleep that is properly and appropriately enjoyed revitalizes the body with happiness and long life — just as a true insight comes to a yogi who is properly disciplined.

text:
( १८४ )
चरकसंहितायाम् ।
Digitized By Siddhanta eSangoti Gyaan Kosha

और वही युक्तिसे कीहुई निद्रा-देहमें-
सुख और अवस्थाको इसप्रकार करतीहै
जैसे बुद्धि–योगी पुरुषको सिद्धि सहित
अपने समागमसे करतीहै ॥ ३८ ॥

गीताध्ययनमघस्त्रीकर्मभाराध्व
कर्षिताः । अजीर्णिनःक्षताःक्षी
णावृद्धाबालास्तथाबलाः॥ ३९ ॥

गाना अध्ययन–मदिरा–स्त्रीका भोग–
भार और मार्ग–इनसे कर्षित मनुष्य अजी-
र्णी-क्षत-क्षीण–वृद्ध-बाल-निर्बल॥ ३९ ॥

तृष्णातीसारशूलार्चोश्वासिनः
शूलिनःकशाः । पतिताभिहतो
न्मत्ताःक्रान्तायानप्रजागरैः।४० ।

तृष्णा-अतीसार-शूल-इनके रोगी श्वास
और शूलरोगी–कृश–पतित–अभिहत
और उन्मत्त–गमन–और जागरणसे ४०

कोधशोकभयक्लान्तादिवास्वमो
चिताश्वये । सर्वेएतेदिवास्वमंसे
वेरन्सार्वकालिकम् ॥ ४१ ॥

और क्रोध–शोक–भयसे–तथा मोह-
से ग्लानिको प्राप्त हुए और दिनमें
शयनके अभ्यासी–इतने मनुष्य दिनमें
सब कालमें शयन करें ॥ ४१ ॥

धातुसाम्यात्तथाहेषांबलञ्चा
प्युपजायते । श्लेष्मापुष्यतिचा
ञ्ञिनिस्थैयर्यंभवितचायुषः॥ ४२ ॥

जिनके धातुकी समानता है और

जिनके बलहै–और कफसे अंग जिनके
पुष्ट हैं और अवस्थामें धीरता है ॥ ४२ ॥

श्लेष्माचादानरूक्षाणांवर्द्धमाने
चमारुते । रात्रीणांचातिसंक्षे
पाद्दिवास्वभःप्रशस्यते ॥ ४३ ॥

और रूक्ष पदार्थोंके सेवनसे पवनकी
वृद्धि है और कफ–स्थिर है रात्रियोंका
संक्षेप है ऐसे समयमें दिनका सोना
उत्तम है ॥ ४३ ॥

ग्रीष्मवज्येषुकालेषुदिवास्वभात्
प्रकुप्यतः। श्लेष्मिपत्तेदिवास्वभ
स्तस्मात्तेषुनशस्यते ॥ ४४ ॥

ग्रीष्मसे भिन्न कालोंमें दिनके सोनेसे
कफ और पित्त कुपित होते हैं तिससे
उन कालोंमें दिनका सोना श्रेष्ठ नहीं ४४

मेदस्विनःश्लेहिन्याःश्लेष्मलाः
श्लेष्मरोगिणः । दूषीविषाचार्श्च
दिवानशयीरन्कदाचन॥ ४५ ॥

मेदस्वी–नित्य स्नेहके अभ्यारी छे-
ष्मल–छेष्मरोगी–दूषी–और विषसे
आर्त ये दिनमें कदाचित् न सोवें॥ ४५ ॥

हलीमकःशिरःशूलस्तैमित्यंगुरुगा
त्रता । अङ्गमर्दोऽग्निनाशश्प्रले
पोहृदयस्यच ॥ ४६ ॥

हलीमक-शिरकाशूल-स्तैमित्य गात्रों
में गुरुता अंगमर्द अग्निका नाश हृदय
का प्रलेप ॥ ४६ ॥
