In the Charaka Samhita.

A completely ignorant person, though posing as learned, should be avoided by the intelligent patient, because such persons are like venomous serpents. ॥ 12 ॥

Those who are learned in the scriptures, skilled, pure, expert in action, controlled in their hands and victorious over their own souls — to them let there always be obeisance. ॥ 13 ॥

And those who are knowers of the scriptures, clever, pure, expert (learned) in action, and who have controlled hands and a controlled soul — to them one should always bow. ॥ 13 ॥ Thus—

Verse therein:

The chapter on the ten seats of life-breath contains a summary of topics of the verses; the two kinds of physicians and the seats of the vital breath have been described. ॥ 14 ॥

Here ends the chapter called Dashapranaayataniya, the twenty-ninth chapter.

The Thirtieth Chapter.
Now we shall explain the chapter called Arthedasha-muliya.
Thus said the Blessed Atreya.

In the matter of meaning (artha), the ten great roots bear great fruit. The wise describe the great meaning using synonyms for the heart. ॥ 1 ॥

In the knowledge of the limbs there are six parts: the five objects of the senses, the soul, and the mind with its qualities — all these worthy of contemplation are situated in the heart. ॥ 2 ॥

The heart is considered the seat of all these states of being for their establishment — just as the central pillar (gopanasi) is the keystone of a house — so say those who reflect on meaning. ॥ 3 ॥

Injury to the heart causes fainting; its piercing leads to death; and the knowledge that perceives touch also resides there, supported by the heart as its sustainer. ॥ 4 ॥

That is the seat of the supreme vital essence (ojas); and there consciousness [the text continues on the next page]

text:
Digitized By Siddha Gyan Kosha ( ३०१ )

संग्रहः ॥ हृदयंमहदर्थश्वतस्मादुकंचिकित्सकैः ॥ ५ ॥

उससे परे ओजका स्थानहै और वहां ही चैतन्यका संग्रहहै, तिससे चिकित्सक हृदय और महान् अर्थ इसको कहते हैं ॥ ५ ॥

तेनंमूलेनमहतामहामूलामताद श ॥ ओजोवहाःशरीरेवाविवध्यन्तेसमन्ततः ॥ ६ ॥

तिस महान् मूलसे दश महामूल माने हैं, तेजके बाहिर वा शरीरमें चारों धमन (प्रकाश) करते हैं ॥ ६ ॥

येनौजसावर्त्यन्तिमृिणताःसर्वदेहिनः ॥ यदतेसर्वभूतानांजीवितंनावतिष्ठते ॥ ७ ॥

जिस ओजसे तृप्त हुये संपूर्ण देही वर्तते हैं और जिसके बिना संपूर्ण भूतोंका जीव नहीं टिकताहै ॥ ७ ॥

यत्सारमादौगर्भेस्ययोऽसौगर्भेर साद्रसः ॥ संवर्ध्मानंहृदयंसमाविशतियत्पुरा ॥ ८ ॥

और जो प्रथम गर्भका सारहै और जो गर्भके रससे रसरूपहै, और जो वर्तमान हृदयमें पहिले प्रविष्ट होताहै ॥

यस्यनाशाच्चनाशोऽस्तिधारियहृदयाश्रितमृ ॥ यःशरीररसःस्नेहःप्राणायत्रप्रतिष्ठताः ॥ ९ ॥

जिसके नाशसे नाश होताहै जो हृदयमें स्थित होकर देहका धारकहै और जो शरीरका रस स्नेहहै जिसमें प्राण टिकताहै ॥ ९ ॥

तत्फलाविविधावाताःफलन्तितिमहाफलाः ॥ ध्यानाद्धमन्यःश्रवणात्स्रोतांसिसरणाच्छिराः १० ॥

उसकी फलसे महाफलवाली विविध वात फलती हैं और धमन कीहुई धमनी श्रवणसे श्रोत, सरणसे शिरा फलती हैं ॥ १० ॥

तन्महानामहामूलास्तचौजःपरिरक्षता ॥ परिहार्योविशेषेणमसोदुःखहेतवः ॥ ११ ॥

वह महान् हैं वे महाफलहैं वह ओज सर्वतःरक्षकहै, विशेषकर मनमेंसे दुःखके हेतु त्यागने योग्यहैं ॥ ११ ॥

हृयंयत्स्यायदौजस्यंस्रोतसांयत्मसादनम् ॥ तत्तत्सेव्यंभ्रयत्नेनप्रशमोज्ञानमेवच ॥ १२ ॥

जो हृदयको ओजको प्रिय हो और स्रोतोंको जो प्रसन्न करे, उस शांति और ज्ञानका प्रयत्नसे सेवन करे इति १२

अथखलुएकंप्राणवर्धनानामुत्कृष्टतमेकंबलवर्धनानामेकंबुंह णानामेकंनन्दनानामेकंहर्षणानामेकमयनानामिति । तत्राहिं साप्राणिनांप्राणवर्धनानामुत्तरु

[Verse 5] The heart is the great seat of meaning; thus physicians regard it as the supreme [organ]. || 5 ||

Beyond it lies the seat of ojas, and there consciousness is gathered; therefore physicians call the heart the great seat of meaning. || 5 ||

[Verse 6] From that great root, the ten great roots [arise]; the channels carrying ojas spread through the body in all directions. || 6 ||

From that great root, ten great roots are recognized; they illumine and radiate outward and throughout the body in all four directions. || 6 ||

[Verse 7] By which ojas all embodied beings are nourished and satisfied; without which the life of all living beings cannot be sustained. || 7 ||

By which ojas all beings in their bodies are satisfied, and without which the life-breath of all living beings cannot be maintained. || 7 ||

[Verse 8] That which is the essence of the embryo from the very beginning, being of the nature of the concentrated essence of the embryonic fluid, enters the heart first. || 8 ||

That which is the primary essence of the embryo, which is itself the refined extract of embryonic fluid, is the first to enter and take up residence in the present heart. || 8 ||

[Verse 9] With whose destruction there is destruction — it dwells in the heart and sustains the body; it is the moistening essence of the body in which the life-breath is established. || 9 ||

When this is destroyed, destruction follows; residing in the heart, it upholds the body; it is the unctuous essence of the body, the very seat in which life-breath is established. || 9 ||

[Verse 10] From it, the many great vatas (channels of movement) bear great fruits; from the dhaman (large vessels) the srotas (channels) branch, and from the srotas the shiras (veins) extend. || 10 ||

From it, the many varieties of vata produce great results; the dhaman vessels generate the srotamsi, and from the srotamsi the shiras spread outward. || 10 ||

[Verse 11] Those great ones among the great roots — the ojas protects all; one should especially abandon whatever becomes the cause of suffering in the mind. || 11 ||

Those are the great ones, they yield great fruit; the ojas protects all beings everywhere. One should especially renounce whatever causes suffering to the mind. || 11 ||

[Verse 12] Whatever is pleasing to the heart and to the ojas, and whatever gladdens the channels — one should carefully and diligently seek that, along with peace and knowledge. || 12 ||

Whatever pleases the heart, nourishes the ojas, and brings joy to the channels — one should pursue that with diligent effort, together with inner peace and wisdom. || 12 ||

Now, there is one supreme among those that increase the life-breath, one among those that increase strength, one among those that nourish, one among those that bring delight, one among those that bring joy, one among those that are paths [to well-being]. Among these, non-violence toward living beings is the foremost among those that increase the life-breath...

translation:
( 302 )
In the Charaka Samhita

The eighth. Of those that increase vital force. Of those that increase strength through virility. Of those that nourish and build the body — the conquest of the senses is the joy-giver. Of those that cause happiness — the knowledge of truth. And brahmacharya is held supreme among the means of right conduct — thus declare those who know Ayurveda. (13)

And among the enhancers of vital force, one (principal) is supreme; among the strengtheners, one; among the nourishers, one; among the joy-givers, one; among the promoters of happiness, one; and among the ways of conduct, one. Among these: non-violence toward all living beings is the highest among enhancers of vital force; virility is the highest among strengtheners; nourishing food among nourishers; conquest of the senses among givers of joy; knowledge of truth among promoters of happiness; and brahmacharya is supreme among the paths of conduct — so the knowers of Ayurveda hold. (13)

Therefore, those who know Ayurveda should be regarded as those who expound the questions of the chapters of the tantra-sthana, sentence by sentence, meaning by meaning, and component by component. (14)

Here the question arises: how do statements from the tantra etc. come to be expounded sentence by sentence, meaning by meaning, and component by component? To this it is said: the entire tantra, when spoken in accordance with its proper place, becomes expressed sentence by sentence. When, with the intellect fully entering into the true nature of the meaning, it is expressed through speech endowed with statement of thesis, reason, example, application, and conclusion — speech comprehensible to the threefold type of student's intellect — it becomes expressed meaning by meaning. The difficult meanings that are fixed in the tantra, when expressed through their explanatory elaborations (deliberations), become expressed component by component. Now if the student were to raise this question: of the four Vedas — Rig, Sama, Yajur, and Atharva — which Veda do the Ayurvedic scholars expound? What is life? What is the reason for Ayurveda? Is this Ayurveda eternal or non-eternal? What are its limbs? By whom is it to be studied, and to what purpose? (15)

In this, the disciple asks how the sentences, meanings, and components of the tantra can be properly stated. To this it is replied: the tantra of the sages, fully according to tradition, is expressed also sentence by sentence; entering well into the true nature of the meaning through the intellect, and expressed through speech that contains thesis, reason, example, application, and conclusion, comprehensible to the three types of a student's understanding — it is also expressed meaning by meaning. The difficult meanings fixed in the tantra, expressed through their elaborations (reflections), are also expressed component by component. If the student then asks whether it is the Rig, Yajur, Sama —

text:
सूत्रस्थानम् १
( ३०३ )

अथर्वण नामके चारों वेदोंमें आयुर्वेदको कौनसा वेद आयुर्वेदके ज्ञाता कहतेहैं और आयुः क्याहै और किससे आयुर्वेद है और वह आयुर्वेद क्या शाश्वत ( सनातन ) है वा अशाश्वतहै इसके अंग कौनहैं यह किनको पढने योग्यहै और किस लिये पढना ॥ १५ ॥

तत्रभिषजापृष्टेनैवञ्चतुणमृक्सामयजुरथर्ववेदानांआत्मनोऽथर्ववेदेभिकरादेश्यावेदोऽहाथर्वणः
स्वस्तयनबलिमङ्गलहोमिनियमप्रायश्चित्तोपवासमन्त्रादिपारिग्राहिचिकित्सांभाह । चिकित्साचायुषोहितायोपदिश्यतेवेदञ्चोपदिश्यआयुर्वाच्यम् । तत्रआयुश्चेतनामृत्तिर्जीवितमनुबन्धोधारिञ्च त्येकोऽर्थःतत्रआयुर्वेदयतीत्यायुर्वेदःकथिमत्युच्यतेस्वलक्षणतः
सुखासुखतोहिताहिततःप्रमाणाप्रमाणतश्च । यतश्चायुष्यानायुष्याणिचद्रव्यगुणकर्मोणिवेदयत्यतोऽप्यायुर्वेदः । तत्रआयुष्याणिअनायुष्याणिचद्रव्यगुणकर्मणिकेवलेनोपदेक्ष्यन्ते ॥ १६ ॥

इसप्रकार वैद्यके पूछनेपर कहै कि ऋक् यजुः साम अथर्व वेदोंमें अथर्व वेद आत्माइसकी भक्ति ( भाग ) कही है

क्योंकि अथर्वण वेद स्वस्तिका अयन ( स्थान ) बलि मंगल होम नियम प्रायश्चित उपवास मंत्र आदिके संग्रहसे चिकित्साको कहतारहै और चिकित्सा अवस्थाके हितार्थ उपदेश कीजाती है वेदका उपदेश करके यह वक्तव्यहै, कि उसमें आयुः चेतनाकी प्रवृत्तिहै जीवित अनुबंध और धारीहै यह एकही अर्थ है, तब ( तिसमें ) आयुको जो वेदयित ( जनावे ) उसे आयुर्वेद कहतेहैं, कैसे यह कोई कहै तो कहतेहैं अपने लक्षणोंसे सुख असुखसे हित अहितसे प्रमाण अप्रमाणसे और जिससे आयुष्य अनायुष्यरूप द्रव्य गुण कर्म जो होतेहैं उनको जो जनावे उसे आयुर्वेद कहतेहैं; उसमें आयुष्य और अनायुष्यरूप द्रव्य गुण कर्मोंका केवल तंत्रसे उपदेश करेंगे १६

तन्त्रेणतंत्रायुरुकंस्वलक्षणतोयथाविदिहैवतत्रशारीरमानसाभ्यां
रोगाभ्यामनिभृदुतस्यविशेषेणयौवनवतः समर्थानुगतबलवीर्य्येणौ
रुषपराक्रमस्यज्ञानविज्ञानेन्द्रियेन्द्रियार्थबलसमुदायेवर्त्तमानस्य
परमिद्धिरुचिरविविधोपभोगस्यस
मृद्धसर्वारंभस्ययथेष्टविचारणात्सुखमायुरुच्यतेअसुखमतोविपर्य्येण ॥ १७ ॥

तिसमें यह अयुक्तहै कि स्वलक्षणसे आयुर्वेदहै, यथार्थ रीतिसे यहांही उसमें
translation:
Sutrasthana 1
(303)

Among the four Vedas named after Atharvana, which Veda do the knowers of Ayurveda call the Veda of Ayurveda? What is ayu (life/lifespan)? From what does Ayurveda derive? Is that Ayurveda eternal (sanatana) or non-eternal? What are its limbs? Who is eligible to study it, and for what purpose should it be studied? (Verse 15)

On this matter, when asked by a physician, among the four Vedas — Rig, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva — it is the Atharva Veda that is declared to be the soul-portion (atma-bhaga) of Ayurveda. Because the Atharva Veda, through its collection of svastika rites, ayana (abodes), bali offerings, auspicious rites, homa, regulations, prayaschitta (expiations), fasting, and mantras and so on, expounds medicine. And medicine is taught for the benefit of life (ayu); this teaching is called Ayurveda. Now, in this context, ayu means: consciousness, vital force, continuance of life, and that which sustains — all these are one meaning. That which makes known (vedayati) this ayu is called Ayurveda. How is it to be described? By its own characteristics: through happiness and unhappiness, through benefit and harm, through what is valid and invalid; and because it makes known those substances, qualities, and actions that are life-promoting (ayushya) and life-diminishing (anayushya) — for this reason too it is called Ayurveda. The life-promoting and life-diminishing substances, qualities, and actions will be expounded by this treatise alone. (Verse 16)

By means of this treatise, life is described by its own characteristics as follows: one whose body and mind are free from disease, who is endowed with the strength and vigor of youth, who possesses the strength of purpose, knowledge, wisdom, and the full power of the senses and their objects, who enjoys varied and excellent pleasures, whose every undertaking is prosperous, and who lives according to his own will — such a person's life is called a happy life (sukha ayus). The opposite of this is an unhappy life (asukha ayus). (Verse 17)

In this context, it is not proper to say that Ayurveda is defined merely by its own characteristics — as will be properly explained here within it.

text:
( ३०४ )
चरकसाहितायाम् ।

जो शरीर और मनके रोगोंसे पीड़ित नहीं, विशेषकर यौवनवान्है, बल वीर्य पुरुषार्थ पराक्रम ये जिसमें भलीप्रकार वर्तमानहैं; ज्ञान विज्ञान इंद्रिय इंद्रियार्थ बल इनके समुदायमें वर्तमानहैं; परम ऋद्धि, रुचिर अनेक प्रकारके भोग इनसे जो युक्तहैं; जिसके संपूर्ण आरंभ भलीप्रकार बढे हुयेहैं ऐसे मनुष्यकी यथेष्ट विचारसे आयु सुखरूप कहातीहै इससे विपरीत असुख होतीहै ॥ १७ ॥

हितैषिणःपुनर्भूतानांपरस्वात्उपरतस्यसत्यवादिनःशमपरस्यपरीक्षकारिणोऽप्रमतस्यत्रिवर्गैपरस्परेणानुपहतमुपमेवमानस्यपूजाहॅसपूजकस्यज्ञानविज्ञानोपशमशीलवृस्यश्चोपसेविनःझुनियतरागेण्यांमदमानवेगस्यसततंविविधप्रदानपरस्यतपोज्ञानप्रशमनित्यस्यअध्यात्मिवदस्तत्परस्यलोकिमम्छामुञ्चावेक्ष्यमाणस्यस्मृतिमतिमतोहितमायुरुच्यते । अहितमतो विपर्ययेण ॥ १८ ॥

और जो हितैषी भूतोंका है परायेधनसे निवृत्तहै सत्यवादीहै शममें तत्पर है परीक्षासे कार्य कारीहै अप्रमत्तहै परमेश्वरके स्मरणसे निरंतर त्रिवर्गका सेवक है पूजाके योग्यका पूजक है ज्ञान विज्ञान उपशममें शील है वृद्धोंका सेवक है राग

रोष ईर्ष्यां मद मान इनका वेग नियमित (रोकना) करता हो निरंतर विविध दानोंमें तत्पर हो तप, ज्ञान, शांति, इनको नित्य करता हो, अध्यात्मका ज्ञाताहै अध्यात्ममें तत्परहै इस लोककी और परलोककी अपेक्षा करताहो, स्मृतिमान् हो ऐसे मनुष्यकी आयु हित कहातीहै, इससे विपरीतकी आयु अहित कहाती है ॥ १८

प्रमाणमायुषस्तवर्थेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धिचेष्टादीनांस्वेनाभिभूतस्यविकृतिलक्षणैरुपलभ्यतेअनिमिनैरिदमस्तात्क्षणान्मुहूर्त्तोद्दिवसात्त्रिपञ्चदशसप्तदशद्वादशाहात्पक्षात्मासात्षण्मासात्संवत्सराद्वारुवभावमापत्यतेइति । तञ्चस्वभावःश्रवृत्तेरुपरमोमरणमनित्यतानिरोध इत्येकोऽर्थः । इत्यायुषःप्रमाणमतोविपरीतमप्रमाणमृ ॥ १९ ॥

आयुका प्रमाण तो अर्थ इंद्रिय मन बुद्धि चेष्टा आदिके विकार लक्षण जो अनिमित्त हैं उनसे जाना जाताहै यह इस क्षणसे मुहूर्तसे दिनसे तीन पांच सात दश द्वादश दिनसे पक्षसे मासमें छः मासमें वा संवत्सरसे स्वभावको प्राप्त होजायगा उसमें स्वभाव प्रवृत्तिका उपरम होजायगा मरण अनित्यता निरोध ये एकही अर्थके बोधकहैं यह आयुका प्रमाण है इससे विपरीत अप्रमाणहै ॥ १९ ॥
translation:
( 304 )
In the Charaka Samhita.

One who is not afflicted by diseases of body and mind, who is especially in the prime of youth, in whom strength, vitality, effort, and valor are well established; in whom the faculties of knowledge, science, the senses, and their objects are fully present; who is endowed with supreme prosperity and many fine pleasures; all of whose undertakings have flourished well — such a person's life, by proper consideration, is called happy. The opposite of this is called unhappy. ॥ 17 ॥

That person who is well-wishing toward all beings, who refrains from taking others' wealth, who speaks the truth, who is devoted to peace, who acts after examination, who is not careless, who serves the three aims of life (dharma, artha, kama) without mutual conflict, who honors those worthy of honor and is himself honored, whose nature inclines toward knowledge, science, and tranquility, who restrains the impulses of passion, anger, pride, and arrogance, who is ever engaged in various forms of giving, who is devoted to austerity, knowledge, and calm, who is learned in matters of the self (adhyatma) and devoted to them, who regards both this world and the next with equanimity, who is possessed of memory and wisdom — such a person's life is called beneficial. The opposite of this is called harmful. ॥ 18 ॥

And that person who is well-wishing to all beings, who is free from desire for others' wealth, who is truthful, who is devoted to peace, who performs actions after examination, who is not negligent, who as a servant of the three aims of life through constant remembrance of the Supreme Being, who is a worshipper of those worthy of worship, who is devoted to knowledge, science, and tranquility, who serves the elderly, who regulates the impulses of passion, anger, envy, pride, and arrogance, who is ever engaged in diverse acts of giving, who practices austerity, knowledge, and calm, who is a knower of the inner self and devoted to it, who regards both this world and the next, who is endowed with memory — such a person's life is called beneficial; the opposite is called harmful. ॥ 18 ॥

The measure of life is known through the signs of impairment — of the senses, mind, intellect, and activities — when these arise without apparent cause. From such signs one can know that within a moment, a muhurta, a day, three, five, seven, ten, twelve days, a fortnight, a month, six months, or a year, the natural course will arrive. That natural course — the cessation of activity, death, impermanence, and dissolution — all mean the same thing. This is the measure of life; what is contrary to this is immeasurable. ॥ 19 ॥

The measure of life is known from signs of impairment appearing without cause in the objects of the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the bodily activities. By such signs one can determine that life will reach its natural end within a moment, a muhurta, a day, three, five, seven, ten, twelve days, a fortnight, a month, six months, or a year. The natural cessation of vital activity — death, impermanence, and dissolution — these all convey the same meaning. This is the true measure of life; what is contrary to this is without measure. ॥ 19 ॥

text:
सूत्रस्थानम् । ( ३०५ )

अरिष्टाधिकारेदेहप्रकृतिलक्षणं धिकृत्यचोपदिष्टमायुषःप्रमाणमायुर्वेदे । प्रयोजनञ्चास्यस्वस्थस्य स्वास्थ्यरक्षणमातुरस्यविकारप्रशमनम् । सोऽयमायुर्वेदःशाश्वतो निर्दिश्यतेऽनादित्वात्स्वभावसंसिद्धस्वलक्षणत्वाद्भावस्वभावनित्यत्वाच्च । निहिनापूत्कदाचिदायुषःसन्तानोवृद्धिसन्तानोवाशाश्वतश्चायुषोविदिताऽनादिमचसुखदुःखंसद्रव्यहेतुलक्षणमपरापरयोगादेषचार्थसंग्रहोविभाभ्यते । आयुर्वेदलक्षणमितियत्पुनःगुरुलघुशीतोष्णस्निग्धरूक्षादीनाञ्चद्वंद्वानांसामान्यविशेषाभ्यांवृद्धिहासौ यथोक्तंगुरुभिरश्यस्यमानैगुर्णामुपचयोभवत्यपचयोलघृनामेवेमेवेतरेषामित्येषभावस्वभावोनित्यः । स्वस्वलक्षणञ्चद्रव्याणांपृथिव्यादीनांसन्तितुद्रव्याणिगुणाश्चनित्यानित्याः ॥ २० ॥

अरिष्ट अधिकारमें देहकी प्रकृतिलक्षणके अधिकारके विषय आयुर्वेदमें आयुके प्रमाणका उपदेश कियाहै इस आयुर्वेदका प्रयोजन स्वस्थकी स्वास्थ्यरक्षाहै और आतुरके विकारका प्रशमनहै सो यह आयुर्वेद शाश्वत कहाताहै क्योंकि यह अनादिहै स्वभावसंसिद्ध स्वलक्षणहै भावोंके स्वभाव नित्यहैं; यह बात नहींहै कि कदाचित् आयुका संतान न हुआ हो, वा वृद्धिका संतान न हुआ हो और आयुका ज्ञाताभी शाश्वतहै और सुख दुःख और द्रव्य, हेतु,लक्षण अनादि हैं पर अपरके योगसे यह अर्थका संग्रह विचारा जाताहै कि आयुर्वेदका लक्षणहै, गुरु,लघु, शीत,उष्ण, स्निग्ध, रूक्ष आदिं जो द्वंद्वहैं उनके सामान्य विशेषोंसे वृद्धि और ह्रासं होते हैं,सोई कहा है,गुरु अभ्यासोंसे गुरुओंका उपचय और लघुओंका अपचय होताहै इसीप्रकार इतरोंका समझना यह भावका स्वभाव नित्यहै और पृथिवी आदि द्रव्योंका स्वलक्षणहै और द्रव्यहैं और गुण नित्य अनित्यहैं॥ २०॥

निहआयुर्वेदस्याभूत्वोत्पात्तिरूप लभ्यते । अन्यत्रावबोधोपदेशाभ्यामेतद्वैद्यमधिकृत्यउत्पत्तिमुपिदशन्त्येकेस्वाभाविकञ्चास्यलक्षणमधिकृत्ययदुक्तिमहचायेऽध्यायेयथाग्नेरौष्ण्यमपांद्रवत्वंभावस्वभावनित्यत्वमपिचास्य यथोक्तंगुरुभिरश्यस्यमानैगुर्णामुपचयोभवत्यपचयोलघूनामित्येवमादि ॥ २१ ॥

translation:
Sutrasthana (Chapter on Fundamental Principles) — Page 305

In the section on Arista (signs of death), after treating the characteristics of bodily constitution (prakriti), Ayurveda has prescribed the measure of lifespan (ayus). The purpose of this science is: for the healthy person, preservation of health; and for the sick person, alleviation of disease. This Ayurveda is declared to be eternal, because it is beginningless (anadi), self-established in its own intrinsic characteristics (svalakshana), and because the nature of all existents (bhavas) is permanently fixed. It is not the case that the lineage of life ever failed to exist, or that the lineage of growth ever failed to exist. The knower of life too is eternal. Happiness, suffering, substance, cause, and characteristic mark — all are beginningless. Yet it is through the association of successive elements that this body of knowledge is gathered and examined: this is the definition of Ayurveda. The pairs of opposites — heavy and light, cold and hot, unctuous and dry, and so on — bring about increase and decrease through their universal (samanya) and particular (visesha) qualities respectively. As it has been said: by habitual use of heavy substances there is increase (upachaya) of heavy qualities and decrease (apachaya) of light qualities; and similarly for the rest. This is the eternal nature of existents. The intrinsic characteristics of substances such as earth and so on are fixed; substances exist, and their qualities are both eternal and non-eternal. || 20 ||

Ayurveda does not arise from something that did not previously exist and then come into being. Elsewhere, through instruction in knowledge, certain authorities, treating this subject from the standpoint of the physician, describe its origin; and treating its intrinsic characteristic, as stated in the relevant chapter — just as heat is the nature of fire and fluidity is the nature of water — the eternal nature of existents is also its character. As it has been stated: through the habitual use of heavy substances, increase of heavy qualities occurs and decrease of light qualities occurs — and so on in this manner. || 21 ||

( ३०६ )

और आयुवेंदकी हो करके पुनः उत्पति नहीं देखतेंहैं अवबोध ( ज्ञान ) और उपदेश तो अवश्य होंतेंहैं; इनही दोनोंका अधिकार करके कोई उत्पति-कामी उपदेश करतेंहैं स्वभाविक जो इसका लक्षणहै वह अकुतक ( नित्य ) है; जो यहां प्रथम अध्यायमें कहाहै कि जैसे अग्निकी उष्णता, जलोंका द्रवत्व और भावोंके स्वभावकी नित्यताहैं; सोई कहाहै कि गुरु अभ्यासोंसे गुरुओंका उपचय और लघुओंका अपचय होताहै इत्यादि ॥ २१ ॥

तस्यायुर्वेदस्य अङ्गानि अष्टौ । तद्यथा । कायचिकित्साशालाक्यंशल्यापहर्तृकंविषगरवैरोधिकप्रशमनंभूतविद्याकौमारभृत्यकं रसायनानिंवाजीकरणमिति । स चाध्येतव्योब्राह्मणराजन्यवैश्यैः। तत्रानुग्रहार्थंप्राणिनांब्राह्मणैरात्मरक्षार्थंराजन्यैर्वृत्त्यर्थंवैश्यैःसामान्यतोवाधर्मार्थिकामप्रतिग्रहार्थंसवैंः । तत्रचयदध्यात्मिवेदांधर्मेप थस्थानांधर्मप्रकाशानांवामातृपितृभातृबन्धुगुरुजनस्यवाविकारप्रशमनेप्रयत्नवान्भवति । यश्चायुर्वेदोक्तमध्यात्ममनुध्यायत्यैत्यधीतेवासोऽप्यस्यपरोधर्मः २२

तिस आयुवेंदके अष्ट अंगहैं; वे ऐसेंहैं कि कायचिकित्सा, शालाक्य, शल्याप-हर्तृक, विष गरके विरोधका प्रशमन, भूतविद्या, कौमारप्रभृत्यक , रसायन, वाजीकरण; इति वह आयुवेंद ब्राह्मण, क्षत्रिय, वैश्योंको पढने योग्य है; उनमें प्राणियोंके अनुग्रहार्थं ब्राह्मण पढें; रक्षाके लिये क्षत्रिय और जीविकाके लिये वैश्य पढें अथवा सामान्यसे सम्पूर्ण धर्म, अर्थ, कामके लिये पढें उनमें अध्यात्मके ज्ञाता धर्ममार्गमें स्थित धर्मके प्रकाशक इनके और माता, पिता, भ्राता, गुरुजनके विकारकी शान्तिमें जो प्रयत्नवान् होताहै और जो आयुवेंदमें उक्त अध्यात्मका ध्यान करताहै; जानताहै वा पढताहै; वहभी इसका परम धर्म है ॥ २२ ॥

यापुनरीश्वराणांवसुमतांवासकाशात्सुखोपहारिनिमित्ताभवत्यर्थलवा वाितरवेक्षणञ्चयाचस्वपरिगृहीतानांप्राणिनामातुष्यद्रिक्षाक्षमत्वञ्चास्यार्थः । यत्पुनरस्यविद्वदग्रहणंयशःशरण्यत्वंयाचसमानशुश्रूषायचेष्टानांजनानामारोग्यमाधत्तेसोऽस्यकामइति ॥ २३ ॥

और राजा धनवान् इनके सकाशसे सुखके उपहार ( भेट ) निमित्तसे, धनके लेशकी प्राप्ति होतींहैं और अवेक्षणहैं और जो अपने परिग्रहके प्राणी हैं; उनकी
translation:
(306)

And those who have attained Ayurveda do not see rebirth; knowledge and instruction certainly arise. Having mastered both of these, those who desire propagation give instruction. What is its natural characteristic is that it is akutaka (eternal); as stated in the first chapter: just as the heat of fire, the liquidity of water, and the inherent nature of things are eternal — so it is said that through practice, the great become greater and the lesser diminish, and so forth. ॥ 21 ॥

The eight limbs of Ayurveda are as follows: Kaya-chikitsa (general medicine), Shalakya (treatment of the head and sense organs), Shalya-pahartrika (surgery), Visha-gara-vairodhika-prashamana (treatment of poisons and antidotes), Bhuta-vidya (psychiatry/spirit medicine), Kaumara-bhritya (pediatrics), Rasayana (rejuvenation therapy), and Vajikarana (aphrodisiac therapy). This Ayurveda is to be studied by Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas. Among them, Brahmanas should study it for the benefit of living beings, Kshatriyas for self-protection, and Vaishyas for livelihood; or all may study it generally for the sake of dharma, artha, and kama. Among them, one who is a knower of the spiritual self, established on the path of dharma, an illuminator of dharma, and who strives to cure the ailments of one's mother, father, brother, and teachers — and who meditates upon, knows, or studies the spiritual teaching declared in Ayurveda — for such a person too, this is the supreme duty. ॥ 22 ॥

As for one who, through proximity to lords and wealthy persons, becomes an instrument for providing pleasant gifts and gains even a small amount of wealth — and who also watches over the living beings under his own and others' care with the capacity to protect them — that is his artha (material gain). And as for one whose wisdom earns him renown, who becomes a refuge for supplicants, who strives to serve people, and who bestows health upon them — that is his kama (fulfillment of desire). ॥ 23 ॥

And from kings and wealthy persons, small amounts of wealth are obtained as gifts for pleasure, and there is care and protection for the living beings who are under one's own household —

translation:

Mantra-sthana
(307)

The capacity to protect from disease is also the purpose of Ayurveda; and teaching Ayurveda to learned scholars, earning fame, protecting those who seek refuge, rendering equal and attentive service, and maintaining freedom from disease with respect to desired objects — all these too are its aims. (23)

As fully stated in response to the question: the eight types of physicians and related matters constitute eight divisions. Namely: the tantra (treatise), the meaning of the tantra, the sthanas (sections), the meaning of the sthanas, the adhyayas (chapters), the meaning of the adhyayas, the prashnas (questions), and the meaning of the prashnas. (24)

When questioned, all of this is to be explained completely — sentence by sentence, meaning by meaning, and component by component. (25)

In that tradition, Ayurveda, shakha, vidya, sutra, jnana, shastra, rakshana, and tantra are all synonyms for one another. The meaning of tantra, as defined by its own characteristics, when examined through its topics (prakaranas), encompasses many things: the functioning of the body, causes, disease, action, effect, time, agent, and instrument — the determination of all these constitutes ten prakaranas, and they will be taught through the tantra alone. (26)

The tantra has eight sthanas (divisions), as follows: Sutra-sthana, Nidana-sthana, Vimana-sthana, Sharira-sthana, Indriya-sthana, Chikitsa-sthana, Kalpa-sthana, and Siddhi-sthana. Of these, the Sutra-sthana has thirty chapters; Nidana, Vimana, and Sharira each have eight chapters; the Indriya-sthana has twelve chapters; the Chikitsa-sthana has thirty chapters; and the Kalpa and Siddhi-sthanas have twelve chapters each. (27)

The tantra has eight sthanas: Shloka-sthana (Sutra-sthana), Nidana, Vimana, Sharira, Indriya, Chikitsa, Kalpa, and Siddhi. Among them, the Shloka-sthana has thirty chapters; Nidana, Vimana, and Sharira have eight chapters each; the Indriya-sthana has twelve chapters; the Chikitsa-sthana has thirty chapters; and the Kalpa and Siddhi-sthanas together have twelve chapters.

( 308 )

Siddhi; these two sections each have twelve chapters. ॥ 27 ॥
And here it is stated:
The thirty-two, the twelve, the three sets of three, and the eights — these are enumerated in the Shloka, Aushadha, Arishta, Vikalpa, Siddhi, Nidana, Mana, and Ashraya [sections]. ॥ 28 ॥
In this work the verses are distributed thus — for each section, groups of thirty, twelve, twelve, and three; and within these the entire text is accounted for: the eight divisions called Shloka, Aushadha, Arishta, Vikalpa, Siddhi, Nidana, Mana, and Ashraya. ॥ 28 ॥
Each section's subject matter will be taught in its proper place. Now hear the names of the one hundred and twenty chapters in order. ॥ 29 ॥
Dirgha-jivitiya, Apamargatanduliya, Aragvadhiya, and the six Virekaashraya — these four form the Bheshaja (medicine) group. ॥ 30 ॥
Matra, Matrashitiya, Vega-non-suppression, and Indriyopakrama — these four chapters belong to the Swasthya-vritti (health regimen) group. ॥ 31 ॥
Khudddaka, Chatushpada, Mahan-trikshaishaṇa, and Vatakalaap — these four are for the guidance of the wise. ॥ 32 ॥
Snehana, Svedana, [their related] chapters, Upakalpana, and Chikitsa-prabhrita — all of these are Upakalpana (preparatory treatment) chapters. ॥ 33 ॥
Kiyantas-shirasiya, Trishopha, Ashtodara, and the great Rogadhyaya — these four constitute the Rogadhyaya (disease chapter) group. ॥ 34 ॥
Ashtau-ninditiya, Langhanatarpaniya, and Vividha-shonitika — these four are described as the Yojana (application) group. ॥ 35 ॥

[Verse 36] — The chapters on Annapanaka and Vividhashitapita, along with the others, make four chapters that settle the matter of food and drink.

Yajnapurushaka, Bhadrakapya, Annapanaka, and Vividhashitapita — these four chapters deal with the determination of food and drink. (36)

[Verse 37] — The chapter "Dashapranayatinika" and likewise the "Dashamulika" — these two are said to support the life-force (prana) and the body, serving as the basis of the physician's qualities.

Dashapranayatinika and, similarly in meaning, Dashamulika — both of these are described as the support of the physician's qualities, serving the life-force and the body. (37)

[Verse 38] — Aushadha (medicine), Svastha (health), Nirdesa (instruction), Kalpana (formulation), Roga (disease), Yojana (application) — these form six groups of four (chatushkas), and the seventh is the Annapanaka chatushka.

Aushadha, Svastha, Nirdesa, Kalpana, Roga, and Yojana — these six chatushkas, and the seventh, the Annapanaka chatushka, have been described in order. (38)

[Verse 39] — The two other chapters are in the nature of a compendium, making thirty chapters in total; these serve the purpose of therapeutics. This Sloka-sthana is declared to be the auspicious head of this treatise.

And two other chapters are compilatory; these thirty chapters serve the purposes of treatment. This Sloka-sthana is called the foremost head of this text. (39)

[Verse 40] — In this section, the great meanings of the four groups (chatushkas) have been compiled. Because the meanings of the verses and their summary are gathered here, it is remembered as Sloka-sthana.

And in this Sloka-sthana, there is great meaning — the determination of these chatushkas is stated here. For this reason it is called Sloka-sthana. (40)

[Verse 41] — Here the meaning and summary of the verses is given, and the topics covered include: fevers, bleeding disorders, abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary disorders (prameha), skin diseases (kushtha), wasting (shosa), mental derangement (unmada), and epilepsy (apasmara).

(41)

[Verse 42] — Thus this group of eight chapters is called the Nidana-sthana (Section on Etiology), as it describes the causes of these diseases — in the matter of tastes (rasas), in the three types of abdominal disorders, and in the destruction of communities (janapada). (42)

[Verse 43] — These are treated in three kinds of disease-knowledge, and they also operate among the seasons, in the form of disease-armies (roganika), among diseases, and in the realm of medical treatment (bhishajita). (43)

[Verse 44] — The great sage has described eight Vimanas (measures/standards) for the purpose of mensuration, including the Katidha-purushiya (how many kinds of persons) and what is incomparable by lineage (gotra). (44)

The chapters on complexion and voice, on flowers, on examination by touch, likewise on the sense-faculties, and on premonitory signs. || 47 ||

का और छटा, कुतवेधनमें ॥ ५७ ॥
श्यामात्रिवृतयोःकल्पस्तथैवचतु
रंगुलेः । तिल्वकस्यसुधायाश्च
सप्तलाशंखिनीष्वपि । दन्तीद्रव
न्त्योःकल्पश्चद्वादशोऽयंसमाप्य
ते ॥ ५८ ॥
श्यामा और त्रिवृत्ताका कल्प, तैसेही
चतुरंगुलमें, तिलकका सुधाका सप्तला
शंखिनीयोंमें दंती द्रवंती यह द्वादशवां
कल्प समाप्त करतेहैं ॥ ५८ ॥

कल्पनापञ्चकर्माण्याबिस्तमूत्रा
तथैवच ॥ स्नेहव्यापादिकासिस
द्धिनेत्रव्यापादिकातथा ॥ ५९ ॥
पंचकर्म नामकी कल्पना, और बस्ति
मूत्रा और स्नेहव्यापादिका सिद्धि और
नेत्र व्यापादिका सिद्धि ॥ ५९ ॥
सिद्धिःशोधनयोश्चैवबस्तिसिद्धि
स्तथैवच ॥ प्रासूतीमर्मसंख्या
तासिद्धिर्बस्त्याश्रयाचया॥६०॥
शोधनोंकी सिद्धि और बस्तिकी सिद्धि
प्रासूती मर्म नामकी और बास्तिके आश्र
यकी सिद्धि ॥ ६० ॥
फलमात्रातथासिद्धिःसिद्धिर्दो
तरसंज्ञिता ॥ सिद्धयोद्वादशैवै
तास्तन्त्रञ्चासुसमाप्यते ॥ ६१॥
फल मात्राकी सिद्धि उत्तरनामकी
सिद्धि ये बारह सिद्धिहैं इनमें इस तंत्रको
समाप्त करतेहैं ॥ ६१ ॥
स्वेस्वेस्थानेतथाध्यायेचाध्याया
र्थःप्रवक्ष्यते ॥ तंब्रूयात्सर्वतः
सर्वंयथास्वंह्यर्थसंग्रहात् ॥६२॥
अपने २ स्थान और अध्यायमें
अध्यायका अर्थ कहेंगे उस तंत्रको सबके
प्रति और सबको यथायोग्य अर्थ संग्र-
हसे कहै ॥ ६२ ॥
पृच्छातन्त्राधथाभ्रायंविविधना
प्रश्नउच्यते ॥ प्रश्नार्थेयुक्तिमां
स्तस्यतन्त्रेणैवार्थिनश्चयः ॥६३॥

Verse 54: [The kalpa chapter treats conditions such as] dvir-niya (bi-doshic conditions), unmada (insanity), apasmara (epilepsy), kshata (wounds/injury), shotha (edema), udara (abdominal disorders), grahani (digestive disorders), and pandu-roga (anemia/jaundice). (54)

Verse 55 (Sanskrit): In hiccough, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, thirst, and in poisoning, and in the three vital points (marmas), and in weakness of the thighs, along with vata and vata-shonika (hemorrhagic vata disorders). (55)
Verse 55 (commentary): Hiccough, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, thirst, and poison, the three vital marma points, weakness of the thighs, vata, and vata-shonika. (55)

Verse 56 (Sanskrit): Thirty treatments, and the disorders of the yoni (female reproductive tract), together with their complications. (56)
Verse 56 (commentary): Thirty treatments and the disorders and complications of the yoni. (56)

Verse 57 (Sanskrit): The kalpa (pharmaceutical preparation) of phala (fruit), jimuta, and ikshvaku is described here, as is that of dhamargava (anga); the fifth is that of vatsaka, and the sixth is that of kutavedha. (57)
Verse 57 (commentary): The kalpa of phala, jimuta, ikshvaku, and of dhamargava (anga), and the fifth kalpa of vatsaka (bark of kutaja), and the sixth pertaining to kutavedhana. (57)

Verse 58 (Sanskrit): The kalpa of shyama and trivrita, and similarly that of chaturangula; of tilvaka and sudha, and also of saptala and shankhini; and the kalpa of danti and dravanti — this twelfth kalpa is hereby concluded. (58)
Verse 58 (commentary): The kalpa of shyama and trivritta, and likewise in chaturangula, the sudha of tilaka, in the saptala and shankhini group, danti and dravanti — thus the twelfth kalpa is concluded. (58)

Verse 59 (Sanskrit): The conception of the five therapeutic procedures (panchakarma), and likewise of basti (enema) and mutra (urinary), and the accomplishment of the treatment of oleation disorders, and likewise that of the treatment of eye disorders. (59)
Verse 59 (commentary): The conceptual section called Panchakarma, and basti-mutra, and the accomplishment of oleation-disorder treatment, and the accomplishment of eye-disorder treatment. (59)

Verse 60 (Sanskrit): The accomplishment of the purification therapies, and also the accomplishment of basti, and likewise the enumeration of prasuti (obstetric) marmas — their accomplishment is dependent on basti. (60)
Verse 60 (commentary): The accomplishment of the purificatory therapies, and the accomplishment of basti, and the section called prasuti-marma, and the accomplishment dependent on basti. (60)

Verse 61 (Sanskrit): The accomplishment of phala-matra (fruit-dose), and also what is called the uttara (concluding) siddhi — these twelve siddhis (accomplishments) complete this tantra. (61)
Verse 61 (commentary): The accomplishment of phala-matra and the accomplishment called uttara — these are the twelve siddhis; with these this tantra is concluded. (61)

Verse 62 (Sanskrit): In each respective place and chapter, the meaning of each chapter will be expounded. One should communicate everything to all, comprehensively, according to its appropriate purport and through proper collection of meaning. (62)
Verse 62 (commentary): In each respective place and chapter, the meaning of the chapter will be set forth. The tantra addresses everyone appropriately, conveying meaning to all as befits them, through a proper collection of meaning. (62)

Verse 63 (Sanskrit): What is called a question (prashna) in the context of a tantra is asked in various ways. The determination of meaning for those who seek it should be done through the tantra itself, with well-reasoned and appropriate questions. (63)

text:
( ३१२ )
चरकसंहितायाम्
Digitized By Siddhanta eGangotri Gyaan Kosha

आम्नायके अनुसार जो तंत्रकी पृच्छा
विधिसे हो उसे प्रश्न कहते हैं; प्रश्नका
अर्थ युक्तिमान् है उसके अर्थका निश्चय
तंत्रसे होताहै ॥ ६३ ॥

निरुक्तंतन्त्रणात्तन्त्रेस्थानमर्थ
प्रतिष्ठया ॥ अधिकृत्यार्थमध्या
यनामसंज्ञाःप्रतिष्ठिताः ॥ ६४ ॥

तंत्रणसे इसको तंत्र कहते हैं अर्थको
प्रतिष्ठासे स्थान कहतेहैं; आयके अधि-
कार करनेसे अध्याय नामकी संज्ञा
प्रतिष्ठितहै ॥ ६४ ॥

इतिसर्वंयथाप्रश्नमष्टकंसम्प्रका
शितम् । कात्स्न्येंनचोक्तस्तन्त्र
स्यसंग्रहःसुविनिश्चितः ॥ ६५ ॥

इस प्रकार ये संपूर्ण अष्टक प्रश्नके अनु-
सार प्रकाशित कियेहैं और संपूर्ण रूपसे
निश्चय करके तंत्रका संग्रह कहाहै ॥ ६५ ॥

सन्तिपाछिवकोत्पाताःसंक्षोभंज
नयन्तिये । वर्त्तकानामिवोत्पाताः
सहसैवविभाविताः । तस्माता
न्पूर्वसंजल्पेसर्वत्राष्टकमादिशेत् ६ ६

पाछिविक नामके वे उत्पातहैं जो संक्षो-
भको पैदा करतेहैं वे वर्त्तकोंके उत्पातके
समान सहसा नहीं विचारे जातें तिससे
उनको पहिलेही संजल्पमें संबंत्र अष्टक
का उपदेश करै ॥ ६६ ॥

परापरपरीक्षार्थेनात्रशाब्दविदांव
लम् । शब्दमात्रेणतन्त्रस्यकेव

लस्यैकदेशिकाः । भ्रमन्त्यल्पब
लास्तन्त्रेज्याशब्देनैववर्त्तकाः ६ ७ ।

पर अपरकी परीक्षाके लिये मात्रा
और शास्त्रके ज्ञाताओंका बलहै; तंत्रके
शब्दमात्रसे जो केवल एकदेशको
जानतेहैं, वे अल्प बल जो भ्रमते हैं
वे तंत्रमें ज्या शब्दसे वर्त्तकों के
समानहैं ॥ ६७ ॥

पशुःपशूनांदौर्बल्यात्किश्चिन्मध्ये
वृकायते । समत्वंवृकमासाधप्रकृ
तिंभजतेपशुः ॥ ६८ ॥

पशुओंकी दुर्बलतासे कोई पशु मध्यमें
वृकके समान आचरण करताहै, वह पशु
बलवान् वृकके समीप आनेपर अपनी
पशु प्रकृतिको भजताहै ॥ ६८ ॥

तद्वदज्ञोऽज्ञमध्यस्थःकिश्चिन्मौख
र्यसाधनः। स्थापयत्यात्मात्मा
नमासन्तवासायिभियते ॥ ६९ ॥

तिसी प्रकार अज्ञोंके मध्यमें स्थित
कोइ अज्ञ प्रधान साधन वाला हो जाता
है और अपनेको आत्म स्थापन करताहै
और आत्मके समीप आनेपर भिन्न हो
जाताहै ॥ ६९ ॥

बभ्रुमृढइवोणांभिरवुद्धिर्बहुश्रुतः।
किंवेवक्ष्यतिसंजल्पेकुण्डमेदीज
डोयथा ॥ ७० ॥

मृढ ऊर्णाओंसे बभ्रु(न्यौला)के समान

translation:
( 312 )
From the Charaka Samhita
Digitized By Siddhanta eGangotri Gyaan Kosha

According to the tradition, that inquiry into a treatise which follows the method of questioning is called Prashna (question). The meaning of Prashna is that which is reasoned; the determination of its meaning comes from the treatise itself. || 63 ||

A treatise is called Tantra because it sustains (tantrana) its subject matter; a section (sthana) is so called because it establishes the meaning; a chapter (adhyaya) gets its designation from taking up a particular topic for treatment. || 64 ||

In this manner the entire set of eight topics (ashtaka) has been set forth according to the method of questioning, and the compendium of the treatise has been fully and definitively stated. || 65 ||

There are natural disturbances (pachivika upheavals) that cause great agitation; they manifest suddenly, like the agitations among quails. Therefore, one should teach the Ashtaka in the preliminary discussion on every such occasion. || 66 ||

For the purpose of examining the superior and inferior, the strength here lies with those who truly know the language and the shastra. Those who know only a fragment of the treatise through its mere words are of little strength; they wander astray within the treatise like quails following the call of the jya word. || 67 ||

Among animals, due to weakness, some animal in the middle of a herd behaves like a wolf; but when that animal comes near a truly powerful wolf, it reverts to its own animal nature. || 68 ||

Similarly, an ignorant person situated among other ignorant ones may for a time put on an air of cleverness and establish himself as authoritative; but when he comes near a truly learned person, he is exposed and becomes a different thing altogether. || 69 ||

Just as a dull creature is surrounded and overcome by the wool-bearing animals like a mongoose, so too a person who is without true understanding but is widely read — what will such a one say in a debate? He will be like a hollow-headed Kundamedi. || 70 ||

A dull person, like a mongoose (nyaula) among wool-bearing animals...

अबुद्धि अबहुश्रुत होनेसे संजल्पमें क्या
कहेगा जैसे कुंडभेदीं जड ॥ ७० ॥

सदृनैनैंनिवगृढीयाद्विषगल्पश्रुतैर
पि ॥ हन्यात्प्रश्नाष्टकेनादाविव
तरांस्त्वात्मानिनः ॥ ७१ ॥

सदाचरणोंसे अल्पश्रुत वैद्यको
ग्रहण न करें वह आदिमें ही प्रश्नाष्टकसे
इतर आत्मानियोंको हतता है ॥७१॥

दम्भिनोमुखराह्यज्ञाःप्रभृताबद्ध
भाषिणः ॥ ७२ ॥

दंभी,मुखर,(मुर्ख)अज्ञ,प्रभृत,बद्धभाषी॥
प्रायःप्रायेणसुमुखाःसन्तोयुक्का
ल्पभाषिणः ॥ तत्वज्ञानप्रका
शार्थमहंकारमनाश्रिताः ॥७३॥

और बहुधा प्रायःसुमुख होकर
युक्त अल्प भाषण करतेहैं; तत्वज्ञानके
प्रकाशार्थे जो अहंकारी नहीं हैं ॥७३॥

स्वल्पाधाराज्ञमुखरान्दर्शेयुर्निव
वादिनः ॥ परोभूतेष्वनुकोशस्त
त्वज्ञानेपरादया ॥ ७४ ॥

उन अल्पआधार अज्ञोंमें प्रधान
विवादियोंको न देखें; भूतोंकी अनिंदा
उत्तम है तत्वज्ञानमें परमदया श्रेष्ठ ७४

येषांतेषामसद्वादनिग्रहेनिरताम
तिः ॥ असत्पक्षाशणित्वाचिदं
भपारुष्यसाधनाः ॥ ७५ ॥

जिनमें है उनकी असत् वादके निग्र-
हमें मति निरत होती है, असतपक्षमें
नेत्रआतिं दंभ पारुष्य जिनकेसाधन हैं ७५

भवन्त्यनाभाःश्वेतन्चेपायःपर
विकथनाः ॥ तत्कालपाशसद
शान्वर्जयेच्छास्त्रदूषकान् ७६॥

ऐसे अनात्त प्रायः अपनी तंत्रमें
परमनुष्योंमें छाघा करते हैं तत्काल में
शास्त्रके दूषक पाशकी तुल्य उनको वर्जे
दे ॥ ७६ ॥

प्रशमज्ञानविज्ञानपूर्णाःसेव्याभि
षकमाः ॥ समग्रंदुःखमायातम
विज्ञानेंद्याश्रयमू ॥ ७७ ॥

उत्तम शांति ज्ञान विज्ञानसे पूर्णे जो
उत्तम भिषक् हैं वे सेवनके योग्यहैं अवि-
ज्ञानमें दोनोंमें समय दुःख आजाताहै७७

सुखंसमग्रंविज्ञानेनिवमलेचप्रतिछि
तम् ॥ इदमेवसुदारार्थमज्ञानार्थ
प्रकाशकम् ॥ ७८ ॥

और समग्र सुख निर्मलविज्ञानमें
टिकताहै, इस प्रकार उदार है अर्थ
जिसका और अज्ञानोंको अपना प्रका-
शक ॥ ७८ ॥

शास्त्रंदृष्टिःप्रनशतानांयथैवादित्यम
णडलिमिति ॥ ७९ ॥

यह शास्त्र तिस प्रकार है जैसे नष्ट
दृष्टियोंको सूर्यमंडल इति ॥ ७९ ॥

translation:
( 313 )

[Verse 70]
What will one who is foolish and unlearned say in debate? Like a dull person striking a pot.

[Verse 71]
Even though surrounded by those who are wise and well-versed in the scriptures, such a one should be overcome by the eight-fold questioning at the very outset — he destroys those who consider themselves self-sufficient.

[Verse 72]
Those who are arrogant, garrulous, ignorant, verbose, and incoherent in speech —

[Verse 73]
— yet often appear pleasant-faced, speak little when occasion demands; they are not egoistic, and their purpose is to illuminate the knowledge of truth. Those who are truly knowledgeable speak few but measured words, without ego, for the purpose of revealing the truth.

[Verse 74]
One should not seek out the ignorant and garrulous who have little foundation and are given to contention. Non-maligning of all beings is praiseworthy; supreme compassion is the highest virtue in knowledge of truth.

[Verse 75]
Those whose intellect is engaged in refuting false arguments — their instruments are the display of pride, harshness of speech, and sharp reproof of the opposing party.

[Verse 76]
Such persons, who are generally devoid of self-knowledge, slander others in their own and others' circles. One should avoid those who corrupt the scriptures, for they are like a noose that binds at the right moment.

[Verse 77]
Those physicians who are full of tranquility, knowledge, and wisdom are worthy of service. In the absence of wisdom, suffering comes to both parties in time.

[Verse 78]
Complete happiness rests in pure and perfect wisdom. This alone is the noble purpose — it illuminates even the ignorant.

[Verse 79]
This scripture is to those whose vision has been lost as the solar disc is to those whose sight is destroyed.

text:
( ३२४ )

तत्रश्लोकाः। अर्थेदशमहामूलाः
संज्ञास्तेषांयथारुताः॥ अयनान्ताः
षड्ङ्याश्वरूपंवेदिवदाश्रयत् ८०

इसमें ये श्लोकहैं कि अर्थमें दशमहा
मूलहैं उनकी संज्ञा यथार्थ करीहैं अयन
पर्यंत छः अग्रच और वेदके ज्ञाताओंका
जो रूप है ॥ ८० ॥

सप्तकश्राष्टकश्चैवपरिप्रश्नःसनिर्ण
यः । यथावाच्यंयदर्थंञ्वषड्विधाः
श्चैकदेशिकाः ॥ ८१ ॥

और सप्तक और अष्टक प्रश्न और
निर्णय सहित, जैसे कहना जिसके अर्थ
और जैसे एक देशिकहैं ॥ ८१ ॥

अर्थेदशमहामूलेसर्वमेतत्प्रकाशि
तम् । संग्रहश्चैवमध्यायस्तन्त्र
स्यास्यैवकेवलः ॥ ८२ ॥

दशमहामूल नामके अर्थमें यह सब
प्रकाशित किया है, संग्रह और अध्याय
ये केवल इस तंत्रमें हैं ॥ ८२ ॥

यथासुमनसांसूत्रंसंग्रहार्थिविधी

Here, the terms hetu, nimitta, ayatana, karta, karana, pratyaya, samutthana, and nidana are all synonymous with one another. Of these, the causes are of three kinds: unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects, errors of judgment (prajnaparadha), and the effects of time and season (parinama). From these three kinds and their variants, diseases arise — whether they are of the nature of Vata, Pitta, or Kapha, or of the twofold kinds, namely Rajasa or Tamasa in character. Among these, the words roga, amaya, gada, atanka, yakshma, jvara, and vikara are all synonymous. Its comprehension is through the five means: nidana (causative factors), purvarupa (premonitory symptoms), linga (signs and symptoms), upashaya (therapeutic test), and samprapti (pathogenesis).

translation:
(Page 315 — Nidanasthana)

The term "nidana" means cause; "purvarupa" means the premonitory signs of a disease before it fully manifests; "laksana" means the manifest signs. The term "linga" refers to shape and form, "cihna" means marks, "samsthana" means configuration, and "vyanjana" means expression — all these are synonymous in this context. "Upashaya" means the use of medicines, foods, and regimens that are either directly contrary to the cause of disease or contrary in effect — their result is a sense of comfort or relief. "Samprapti" (pathogenesis), "jati" (category), and "agati" (mode of onset) are all synonymous terms for the process of disease; it is further analyzed by number, predominance, type, variation, strength, and time. "Number" refers to, for example, eight types of fever, five types of gulma (abdominal tumors), seven types of skin disorders, and so on. "Predominance" is determined by comparing the relative degree of the doshas involved — whichever of the two is more prominent is designated as such. "Type" means that diseases are of two kinds by origin — endogenous and exogenous — and of three kinds by doshic involvement; and of four kinds by curability — mild, severe, curable, and incurable. "Variation" (vikalpa) refers to the partial dominance of doshas when they are co-present. "Strength and time" refers to the fact that the strength of a disease is governed by the seasons, day and night cycles, and dietary habits. Therefore, a physician, with his faculties of reasoning and intellect unimpaired, should understand diseases properly in all their aspects. This is the summary of the Nidanasthana; it will be explained in greater detail further on.

First of all, we shall explain the eight diseases arising from the causes of envy, hatred, and anger, in order, beginning with their nidana (causative factors). And we shall similarly explain the general outline of their treatment, and thereafter describe each disease in detail in due order. (Section 1)

(Hindi commentary:) Here it is established that hetu, nimitta, ayatana, karta, karana, pratyaya, samutthana, and nidana are all synonymous — that is, they are all names for nidana. Nidana is of three kinds: unwholesome contact of the sense organs with their objects (asatmya-indriyartha-samyoga), intellectual error (prajnaparadha), and the effects of time (parinama). Correspondingly, diseases too are of three kinds: those of fiery (agneya), watery/lunar (saumya), and wind (vayavya) character. There are also two further types: rajasa and tamasa. Among these, the terms amaya, gada, atanka, yakshma, jvara, vikara, and roga are not different in meaning. Their understanding (knowledge) comes through nidana, purvarupa, linga, upashaya, and samprapti. Of these, nidana means the cause — as already stated. The premonitory sign of a disease before it manifests is purvarupa. The manifest symptom of a disease is linga. In this, linga, akrti, laksana, cihna, samsthana, vyanjana, and rupa are all not different in meaning. In this sense, upashaya is that which...

translation:
( 316 )

The medicines, diet, and regimen that are opposites of the disease and its causative factors, and their comfortable association — the terms "samprapti," "jati," and "agati" do not differ in meaning from one another. Through the distinctions of number, predominance, type, variation, strength, time, and specific form, the classification of diseases is determined — for example, eight types of fever, five types of gulma (abdominal tumors), seven types of kushtha (skin disorders), and so on. Predominance is understood through the lesser or greater presence of the doshas; this is called the "taratama bhava" (the principle of more or less). When comparing two, the suffix "tara" applies; when comparing three, "tama" applies. In this manner, diseases are of two kinds based on the distinction between intrinsic (nija) and extrinsic (agantuja) causes. From the distinction of the three doshas, three types are recognized; from the distinction of curable, incurable, mild, and severe, four types are recognized. The proportional variation in the combined doshas, and the specific quality of strength and time particular to each disease, are governed by the rules of season, day-night cycle, diet, and time. Therefore a physician who wishes to understand diseases correctly must know their causative factors and other characteristics truly. This is the summary of the Nidana Sthana (section on etiology). Its detailed explanation follows hereafter. Therein, beginning with the eight diseases that arise from greed, malice, and anger in the wealthy (adhya), they are described in order with their etiologies, and likewise the summary of therapeutic principles, the later course of treated patients, and the sequential description of the specified disorders are set forth. (Section 1)

Here, fever (jwara) is the first among diseases to be described. Among these, those of bodily origin come first. Now: from eight causes does fever arise in human beings — from vata, from pitta, from kapha, from vata-pitta combined, from pitta-kapha combined, from vata-kapha combined, from all three together (vata-pitta-kapha), and from external (agantuja) causes. We shall describe its etiological features, premonitory signs, characteristic symptoms, and stages of development. Furthermore, through excessive indulgence in rough, light, cold foods; excessive exercise, emesis, purgation, enema, nasal therapy; suppression of natural urges; fasting; physical injury; sexual excess; mental agitation, grief, excessive bleeding, wakefulness, uneven bodily postures — through all these, vata becomes aggravated. When that aggravated vata, combined with heat, enters the site of the digestive fire (amashaya), it obstructs the channels carrying the essence of food, the tissues, and their nourishment, and disrupts the digestive fire at its seat, driving away the body's heat — then fever is produced. Its characteristic signs are: irregular onset, heaviness of the body, and variation in the distribution of heat throughout the body...

translation:
(Page 317 — Nidanasthana, Chapter on Fever/Jwara)

[Left column:]
The manifestations and stages of fever (jwara): toward the end of digestion, at the end of the day, and at the end of sweating, there is aggravation or onset of fever. Its special signs include roughness and redness of color in the nails, eyes, face, urine, feces, and skin; an excessive sense of heaviness; various pains in the limbs, moving and unsteady. In the calves there is cramping; in the knees, a feeling of separation of the joints; in the thighs, weakness; in the waist, sides, back, shoulders, arms, and chest, pain as if broken, crushed, or bruised; a ringing or rattling sound in the ears and temples; an astringent taste in the mouth; a disagreeable taste; dryness of the palate and throat; thirst; a gripping sensation in the heart; dry retching; dry cough; sneezing; inability to retain things; perspiration; loss of taste and appetite; indigestion; despondency; yawning; trembling; delirium; insomnia; horripilation; sensitivity of the teeth — all these arise. Furthermore, there is no proper nourishment from the causes prescribed (for health), but instead their opposite — excessive nourishment from what is contrary. These are the signs of vata-fever. Sour, salty, pungent, undigested foods —

[Right column:]
— when excessively consumed, as well as excessive sharp heat, exertion, anger, and irregular diet: by these pitta becomes aggravated. Then the aggravated pitta, starting from the amashaya (stomach), heats up the digestive fire; blocking the channels that carry the essence of food — rasa, sweat, and the like — with obstructions, it overwhelms the sites of digestion and drives the heat out through the openings, heating the entire body alone, and thus produces fever. Its signs are as follows: the fever comes on and intensifies simultaneously throughout the whole body. In one who has eaten, especially at midday and afternoon, there is a burning sensation, bitterness of the mouth, inflammation of the nose, mouth, throat, and lips, thirst, dizziness, intoxication, fainting, vomiting, diarrhea, aversion to food, exhaustion, perspiration, skin eruptions (kotha), yellowish or greenish discoloration of the body, nails, eyes, face, urine, feces, and skin, an intensely hot feeling, and excessive burning heat. The prescribed causes showing no nourishment but their opposites showing increase — these are the signs of pitta-fever. [Next: signs related to cold, heavy, unctuous, sweet —]

(Page 318 of the Charaka Samhita)

Excessive indulgence in slimy, sour, and salty foods, daytime sleeping, excitement, and physical exercise leads to aggravation of kapha (phlegm). When this aggravated kapha enters the stomach, it mixes with the digestive heat, pervades throughout the nutrient essence of digested food, blocks the channels, suppresses the digestive fire, either drives the heat away from its seat of digestion or expels it outward, and by pressing down on the body alone, it produces fever. These are its signs: simultaneous onset of fever throughout the body, a sense of heaviness, nausea, loss of appetite, increased salivation, sweetness in the mouth, cold sensation, drowsiness, cough, pain in the heart region, heaviness of the eyes, excessive sleep, stiffness, drowsiness, labored breathing, cough, sneezing, coldness, pallor of the eyes, nails, face, urine and skin, excessive cold sensation, eruptions on the limbs, and non-increase of the stated causative factors or their contrary increase — these are the signs of kapha-fever.

From irregular eating, fasting, non-evacuation of the bowels, unwholesome smells inhaled, drinking water hated by the patient, contact with trees of the forest, improper use of emesis, purgation, enemas, head-cleansing therapies, from intercourse with women of forbidden categories, from wrong treatment of the named conditions, and from the combination of the stated causes — from any one of these, or from all three doshas simultaneously becoming aggravated, they then produce fever one after another in due order. By observing the mixed appearance of the signs of the fevers described, one should recognize a particular fever as dual-doshic or sannipata (triple-doshic). The eighth type of fever arises from external causes — from physical injury, demonic affliction, black magic, and curses. For some time it remains as a purely exogenous fever, but afterward it becomes bound to the doshas. The one caused by injury is associated with vitiated blood through the agency of vata; the one caused by demonic affliction is bound by both vata and pitta; those caused by black magic and cursing are bound by sannipata. Since this fever is distinguished from the other seven fevers by its characteristic signs, mode of treatment, and manner of arising, it is to be recognized as distinct.

Page 319 — Nidanasthana (Section on Etiology)

These should be understood through common features of action. Fever (jvara) is thus described as having eight varieties of constitutions. Fever has heat (santapa) as its single characteristic mark; it is described in two ways according to a particular intention — as intrinsic (nija) and extrinsic (agantu). Among these, the intrinsic is described as twofold, threefold, fourfold, and sevenfold, according to the variants beginning with Vata. These are the prodromal signs: bitterness of mouth, heaviness of the limbs, loss of desire for food, disturbance of vision, excess of sleep, restlessness, yawning, trembling, exhaustion, delirium, wakefulness, horripilation, intolerance of sound, music, wind and sun, loss of appetite, indigestion, debility, pain in the limbs, lassitude, loosening of the body, long-windedness, idleness, diminution of work previously undertaken, aversion toward one's own duties, irritability toward teachers' words, hostility toward children, indifference to one's own dharma, aversion to thinking of garlands, ointments, food, and hair-care, aversion to sweets and pleasures, and craving for salt and pungent things — these are the prodromal signs of fever. Because these, beginning with heat, accompany and follow the state of fever and afflict the sufferer, these are the individual symptoms of each type of fever, described in full or in brief.

Fever, verily, arises from the wrath of Maheshvara; it destroys the life-force of all beings; it afflicts the body, senses and mind; it destroys strength, color, joy, enthusiasm; it causes exhaustion, delusion, and suppression of appetite; it burns the bodies — thus is fever. No other disease is as fierce, causing so many complications and so difficult to treat. Fever is the lord of all diseases; it is described by many names in the various forms of life. All living beings are born with fever and die with fever; being overwhelmed by it, they lose their memory of all past deeds; fever alone takes away the life-breath from all creatures.

For one who shows prodromal signs of fever, light food and non-nourishing diet should be prescribed at the outset, since fever arises from the stomach (amashaya). Then, decoctions of astringent herbs, massage, sudation, poultices, ointments, emesis, purgation, enema, anuvasana enema, nasal treatments, medicated smoking, collyrium, and milk-diet should be administered as appropriate. In all cases of chronic (jirna) fever, intake of ghee is recommended. Medicated ghee prepared with appropriate herbs destroys by its processing the kapha and cold that have accumulated, and restores the bodily heat; therefore, in cases of chronic fever —

अग्निमें संताप श्रम क्रोध विषमभोजन
इनसे पित्त कोपको प्राप्त होताहै, वह जब
प्रकुपित हुआ आमाशयसेही ऊष्माके संग

अन्वावेदन ( मेल ) करके और रस

translation:
( 320 )

"In all [substances] that have been combined with water and immersed [in liquid], these [properties apply]." — [Verse] 2

Now, fever (jvara) is spoken of first among all bodily disorders. Being the foremost among the diseases of the body, it arises in human beings from eight causes: from vata (wind), from pitta (bile), from kapha (phlegm), from vata-pitta combined, from pitta-kapha combined, from vata-kapha combined, from vata-pitta-kapha combined, and the eighth cause being external (agantuja). The text proceeds to teach the specific nidana (causative factors), purvarupa (premonitory signs), linga (symptoms), and upachaya (aggravating conditions) of that fever.

The excessive use of the following leads to provocation of vata (wind): rough, light, and cold [foods or substances], exercise, vomiting, purgation, retention enemas, nasal therapies, excessive suppression of natural urges, fasting, physical injury, sexual activity, anxiety, grief, hemorrhage, excessive wakefulness, irregular posture of the body. When provoked, that vata enters the stomach (amashaya), mingles with the bodily heat (ushma), and following the first product of food-digestion known as rasa-dhatu (nutritive fluid), it blocks the channels (srotas) through which rasa and sweat flow. It then drives the heat out of the site of digestion into the body alone, and thus produces fever.

The signs of this [vata] fever are as follows: irregular onset and cessation, unevenness of bodily heat, extreme instability [of temperature], arising and increasing at the end of digestion, at the end of the day, or at the end of perspiration. The fever is characteristically rough and reddish; the nails, eyes, mouth, urine, feces, and skin become discolored. There are many kinds of moving and stationary pains; the knees and joints of various limbs tremble; the thighs feel numb; the loins, flanks, back, shoulders, arms, shoulder-joints, and chest feel as though broken, diseased, crushed, churned, pressed, or struck. The jaw becomes stiff; there is ringing in the ears and continuous shooting pain in the temples; the mouth tastes astringent and unpleasant; the mouth, palate, and throat become dry; there is intense thirst, great dryness in the heart region, cough, sneezing, suppression of belching, distress over the taste of food, excessive salivation, anorexia, indigestion, depression, yawning, fatigue, trembling, exhaustion, delirium, sleeplessness, horripilation, and sensitiveness of the teeth. Likewise, whatever is stated in the nidana as being agreeable (priti) to heat, its diminution — and the increase of its opposites — all these are the signs of vata-fever.

Excessive consumption of hot, sour, salty, alkaline, and pungent foods, as well as of undigested food, and similarly, exposure to intense sunlight, heat from fire, exertion, anger, and irregular eating — these provoke pitta (bile). When provoked, pitta — arising from the stomach itself — mingles with the bodily heat, combines with rasa (the first dhatu, the nutritive fluid that is the product of digested food), blocks the channels carrying rasa and sweat, impairs the digestive fire through its own liquid nature, and afflicting the heat outside the site of digestion, reaches the body alone — [the text continues on the next page].

translation:
When it occurs, it produces fever. Its signs are as follows: the onset or increase of fever in the body happens only once at a time — during the period of digestion of food, at midday, at midnight, at the beginning of the day, or especially in autumn. In the mouth there is bitterness; the throat, lips, and palate feel as if burning; there is thirst, fainting, confusion, loss of consciousness; there is bile-induced purging; aversion to food; exhaustion; perspiration; delirium; eruption of reddish patches on the skin; yellowish-green and golden discoloration of the nails, eyes, mouth, urine, feces, and skin; intense burning heat; and in cold conditions a sensation of internal heat. In the etiology, a decrease of the factors mentioned and an increase of their opposites — these are the signs of pitta-fever.

Oily, sweet, heavy, cold, slimy, sour, and salty substances; sleeping during the day; excessive joy; excessive exercise — when these are used excessively, kapha becomes aggravated. When it becomes aggravated, it enters the stomach, mingles with heat, follows the nutrient substance (rasa) which is the transformation of previously consumed food, and covers the channels that carry rasa and sweat, suppresses the digestive fire, and drives the heat out of its seat of digestion. Afflicting the body heat, it reaches the body alone and then produces fever. Its signs are: the onset or increase of fever in the body occurs only once; it especially occurs immediately after eating, in the forenoon, or in spring. Heaviness of the limbs, absence of desire for food, salivation, sweetness in the mouth, nausea, a coating over the heart, sluggishness, excess of sleep, stiffness, drowsiness, dyspnea, cough, catarrh, chilliness, whitish discoloration, and cold sensation in the eyes, nails, mouth, urine, feces, and skin — an intense cold arising from the limbs, while in warmth there is a drawing sensation — and in the etiology, a decrease of those mentioned and increase of their opposites — these are the signs of kapha-fever.

For those who eat irregularly, through fasting, through change of food, through the influence of the season, through smelling of unwholesome odors, through use of water contaminated by poison, through contact with venomous creatures, through association with mountains, through improper use of oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, enema (āsthāpana and anuvāsana), and nasal therapy, through improper use of these, and through abnormal childbirth in women, and through improper care of mothers after delivery, and through the mixing of the causes mentioned — according to the learned, in dual combinations (dvandva), one or all three doshas together may become simultaneously aggravated. Being aggravated, they produce fever in the same sequence described above. In that fever, by the characteristic mixing of the fever signs as described, one should recognize either a dual-dosha (dvandvaja) or triple-dosha (sannipātaja) fever.

From physical injury (abhighāta), from demonic possession (abhiṣaṅga), from sorcery (abhicāra), and from cursing (abhiśāpa) — from these arises the eighth type, the exogenous fever (āgantu-jvara), in the manner described above. This exogenous fever exists for some time as an independent condition and then becomes associated with the doshas. The abhighāta-type is seated in the blood and is associated with vāyu, and the abhiṣaṅga-type is associated with vāta and pitta.

( ३२२ )

आमिशापज और अभिचारज ये दोनों संनिपातके संग मिल जाते हैं; सात प्रकारके ज्वरसे विशिष्ट जो लिंग उनके उपक्रमसे उत्थित होनेसे यह आगंतु विशिष्ट जानना, कर्मसे साधारणसे उपक्रमसे यह आठ प्रकारकी ज्वरकी प्रकृति कही; ज्वर तो संताप लक्षणका एकही है उसकोही अभिप्रायके विशेषसे और निज आगंतुके विशेषसे दो प्रकार का कहते है उनमें जिनको दो तीन चार सात प्रकारका वात आदिके विकल्पसे कहते हैं उसके ये पूर्वरूप होते हैं वे ऐसे हैं कि मुखका वैरस्य गात्रमें गौरव अन्नकी अनिच्छा नेत्रोंमें व्याकुलता आंसुओंका आना अधिक निद्रा अति जृंभा विनाम कंप श्रम भ्रम प्रलाप जागरण लोमहर्ष, शब्द गीत वात आतप इनका सहना न सहना अरुचि अविपाक दुर्बलता अंगमर्द सदन प्राणोंमें अल्पता; दीर्घसूत्रता आलस्य उपचित भी कर्मकी हानि, अपने कायोंमें प्रतीप बुद्धि गुरुओंके वाक्योंकी असूया बालकोंमें द्वेष अपने धर्मोंमें अचिंता माल्य अनुलेपन भोजन इनमें केश, मधुर पदार्थोमें द्वेष, अम्ल लवण कटु इनमें प्रीति; ये सब ज्वरके पूर्व रूप हैं संताप से पहिले भी इस मनुष्यको संतापसे आर्तको ये अनुबंधन करते हैं इससे ये एक २ ज्वरके लिंगहैं; विस्तार और संक्षेपसे उक्त ज्वर तो निश्चयसे महादेव के कोपसे उत्पन्न है, सब प्राणियोंके प्राणोंका हर्ता, देह इंद्रिय मन इनके तापका कर्ता, मज्ञा बल वर्ण, हर्ष उत्साह सादन आति श्रम क्लम मोह आहार इनके उपरोधको पैदा करता है; जो शरीरोंको जरण करै वह ज्वर कहाताहै; अन्य व्याधि तैसी दारुण बहुत उपद्रवी चिकित्सामें कठिन नहींहै जैसा यह ज्वर है; सब रोगोंका अधिपति, नानाप्रकारकी तिरछी योनियोंमें अनेक प्रकारके शब्दोंसे कहा जाता है; संपूर्ण प्राणधारी ज्वर सहितही पैदा होतेहैं ज्वर सहितही मरतेहैं वह ज्वर महामोहहै तिससे तिरस्कृत हुये देहधारी पूर्वदेहके किंचित्भी कर्मका स्मरण नहीं करते; सब प्राणियोंको ज्वरही लेताहै, तिससे इसके पूर्वरूपके दर्शन होनेपर वा ज्वरकी आदिमें लघु भोजनका अत्यंति; को करै क्योंकि ज्वर आमाशयमें उत्पन्नहै; फिर कषायका पान अभ्यंग स्वेद प्रदेह परिषेक अनुलोमन विरेचन आस्थापन अनुवासन उपशमन नस्तःकर्म ( सूंघना ) धूप धूमका पान अंजन दूधका भोजन इनको करै; यथा योग युक्तिसेसभी जीर्णज्वरोंमें उस घीका पीना श्रेष्ठहै जो यथा योग औषधोंसे सिद्ध हो; क्योंकि घी सेहसे वातको शांत करताहै संस्कारसे कफको शीतलतासे पित्तको और ऊष्माको शांत करताहै; तिससे संपूर्ण जीर्णज्वरोंमें घी ऐसा हित उत्तम है जैसे अग्निसे दग्ध द्रव्योंमें जल होताहै ॥ २ ॥
translation:
( 322 )

Amishapaja (fever born of meat/flesh causes) and Abhicharaja (fever born of black magic/ritual harm) — these two combine with Sannipataja (triple-dosha) fever. The specific signs arising from the treatment approaches of the seven types of fever being present, this is to be understood as Agantuja (exogenous) fever. Through ordinary karmic means, the nature of these eight types of fever has been described. Fever has only one characteristic: heat. By distinction of intent and by distinction of the intrinsic and exogenous types, it is spoken of in two ways. Among those described variously as being of two, three, four, or seven types based on Vata and the other doshas, their prodromal signs are as follows: a bad taste in the mouth, heaviness in the limbs, loss of appetite, restlessness in the eyes, the coming of tears, excessive sleep, frequent yawning, bending of the body, trembling, exhaustion, dizziness, delirium, wakefulness, horripilation; inability to bear sound, song, wind, or sunlight; loss of taste, indigestion, weakness, pain in the limbs, lassitude, diminishment of vital breath; procrastination, laziness, decline even in accumulated duties, a contrary intellect in one's own affairs, contempt for the words of elders, aversion toward children, neglect of one's own dharma, indifference toward garlands, ointments, and food; aversion to hair-care and sweet substances, fondness for sour, salty, and pungent things — all these are the prodromal signs of fever. Even before the heat appears, these bind the afflicted person with distress. Thus these are the individual signs of each fever. To speak briefly and at length: fever surely arises from the wrath of Mahadeva (Shiva). It is the destroyer of the vital breath of all living beings. It is the cause of burning in the body, senses, and mind. It suppresses marrow, strength, complexion, joy, enthusiasm, and causes weakness, exhaustion, fatigue, stupor, and obstruction of food. That which causes the body to age (jara) is called Jvara (fever). No other disease is as terrible, as troublesome in its complications, or as difficult to treat as this fever. It is the lord of all diseases, spoken of by many names in various kinds of existence. All living beings are born with fever and die with fever. That fever is the great delusion; those embodied beings overpowered by it do not remember even a little of the karma of their previous body. Fever takes all living beings; therefore, upon seeing its prodromal signs or at the onset of fever, one should reduce food intake, since fever originates in the stomach (amashaya). Thereafter one should use: decoction-drinking, oil massage, sudation, application of pastes, affusion (pouring water), mild purgation, enema, anuvasana (oil enema), pacifying therapies, nasal administration (snuffing), fumigation, smoke inhalation, collyrium (eye application), and consumption of milk. With appropriate measures and reasoning, in all cases of chronic fever (jirna jvara), the drinking of ghee prepared with suitable medicinal herbs is considered the best, because ghee by its natural quality pacifies Vata, by its processing pacifies Kapha, and by its coolness pacifies Pitta and heat. Therefore, in all chronic fevers, ghee is as beneficial and excellent as water is to things burned by fire. || 2 ||

गीयते । तद्व्यक्तिव्यवसायार्थं
द्विरुक्तःसनगर्हेते ॥ ६ ॥

गद्यमें कहाजो अर्थ है वही अर्थ फिर
श्लोकोंसे कहा जाताहै उसकी व्यक्तिके
निश्चयार्थ द्विरुक्त भी वह निंदायोग्य
नहीं होता ॥ ६ ॥

त्रिविधंनामपञ्यायैंहेतुंपञ्चविधाच्
गदान् । गदलक्षणपञ्यायान्
व्याधेःपञ्चविधंग्रहम् ॥ ७ ॥

पर्यायोंसे तीन प्रकारका हेतु–पांचप्रका
रके–गदके लक्षणके पर्यायोंसे गद–
व्याधिका पांच प्रकारका गृहहै ॥ ७ ॥

ज्वरमष्टविधंतस्यप्रकृटासञ्काः
रणम् । पूर्वरूपञ्चरूपञ्चसंग्रहेमे
षजस्यच ॥ ८ ॥

ज्वर आठ प्रकारका और उत्तम आसन्न
कारण, पूर्वरूप–और रूप इनको भेष
जके संग्रहमें ॥ ८ ॥

व्याख्यातवानृज्वरस्याग्नेनिदाने
विगतज्वरः । भगवानग्निवेशाय
प्रणतायपुनर्वसुः ॥ ९ ॥

इतिचरकप्रतिसंस्कृतेतन्नेज्वरानिदानो
नामप्रथमाऽध्यायः ॥ १ ॥

प्रथम ज्वरके निदानमें–संताप रहित
पुनर्वसु महिषैं भगवान्ने प्रणत ( नम्र )
अग्निवेशके प्रति वर्णन किया ॥ ९ ॥
इति ज्वरनिदानं समाप्तम् अध्याय ॥ १ ॥

द्वितीयोऽध्यायः ।
रक्तपित्तनिदानम् ।
अथातोरक्तपित्तनिदानं
व्याख्यास्यामः ।

इतिह्स्माहभगवानात्रेयः ।
इसके अनंतर रक्त पित्तके निदानका
